references.title: “Neubrutalism is taking over the web”
references.lede: The March 2022 essay usually credited with naming and spreading the style.
references.summary: Michał Malewicz’s description of neubrutalist contrast, hard shadows, colors, and windows.

evidence.note: Full text read from the Wayback capture of 21 April 2022. The page’s embedded data gives a first-published time of 2022-03-28. The live page is now partly paywalled.

styles.note: An early, widely cited text that names the style and sets out its rules for shadows, outlines, and color.

context: Malewicz writes: “Neubrutalism, or Neobrutalism as some people call it, is a mix of regular brutalism in web design and more modern typography, illustration and animation standards.”

On shadows: “The main rule of neubrutalist shadows is to avoid using blur on them.” And: “Instead of soft shadows, it goes for hard, black rectangles under the cards. Instead of typical barely visible borders, it goes for thick, dark and defined outlines.”

He also describes pure black #000000 against color, computer-window motifs, and names Figma and Gumroad as the “two main innovators”. He notes that earlier brutalism “was mostly popular in poster-design / graphics-design”.
The GitHub [Awesome Neobrutalism](https://github.com/ComradeAERGO/Awesome-Neobrutalism) list places it first among articles.
interpretation: The best early attestation for the name. It fixes the diagnostic pair of the style (thick outline and unblurred shadow) and separates it from the raw brutalist web.

rights.statement: Text and images © Hype4 / Michał Malewicz. Link and quotation only.

references.title: “Rosalinde”, plate from the Gazette du Bon Ton
references.lede: George Barbier’s fashion plate of a Worth evening dress, set against a black lacquered commode with gilt mounts, above a centered title in spaced capitals.
references.summary: A slender figure in a fringed gold dress before a black lacquer commode; spaced capitals below. George Barbier, 1922.

source.label: Rijksmuseum: Gazette du Bon Ton, 1922 – No. 10: Rosalinde, RP-P-2009-1964-4

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Rijksmuseum scan from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gazette_du_Bon_Ton,_1922_-_No._10_Rosalinde_Robe_du_soir,_de_Worth,_RP-P-2009-1964-4.jpg) (4254 × 5540 px). The Rijksmuseum record text was read from the Commons copy of its metadata.

styles.note: The Gazette du Bon Ton plates set the look of early Art Deco fashion: stylized slender figures, lacquer and gilt, and centered spaced capitals.

context: The Rijksmuseum lists the plate as Gazette du Bon Ton 1922, No. 10, plate 75: “Rosalinde / Robe du soir, de Worth”, after a design by George Barbier, printmaker anonymous, published by Lucien Vogel with Condé Nast. It describes the technique as photomechanical colour print with letterpress text, sheet 246 × 189 mm. [Commons copy of the Rijksmuseum record](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gazette_du_Bon_Ton,_1922_-_No._10_Rosalinde_Robe_du_soir,_de_Worth,_RP-P-2009-1964-4.jpg).
The Rijksmuseum describes the dress as gold lace decorated with pearls. [Rijksmuseum](https://www.rijksmuseum.nl/en/collection/RP-P-2009-1964-4).
observed: A slim woman with pale skin and blonde hair in a low knot stands at the center, facing left, her hands on the top of a commode.
Her dress is a straight, dropped-waist shift in gold with a diamond pattern, a belt of small geometric blocks in pink and green, and long fringes in blue, green, and gold.
The commode behind her is black with gilt rococo mounts and painted pink roses; a blue bowl with a large flower stands at left and a small bronze nude on a marble base at right.
The ground is plain cream paper with no setting beyond the furniture.
The title “ROSALINDE” is centered below in widely spaced serif capitals, above a smaller line “ROBE DU SOIR, DE WORTH”.
Italic lines at the lower corners read “No 10 de la Gazette” and “Année 1922. — Planche 75”. The signature “GEORGE BARBIER 1922” sits at lower left of the image.
interpretation: The plate is early, pre-1925 Art Deco: the figure is elongated and simplified, the dress is geometric, and the black lacquer and gold give the luxury palette. The commode itself is an eighteenth-century form, which shows how Deco borrowed historical luxury.
The centered title in spaced capitals on plain ground is the typographic habit later seen in Deco posters and packaging.
borrow: Center a short title in widely spaced capitals on plain ground, with a smaller second line below it.
Put one glossy black shape behind a light figure to create the lacquer-and-gold contrast.

images.alt: Fashion plate on cream paper: a slim blonde woman in a gold fringed evening dress stands in front of a black lacquered commode with gilt mounts and painted roses, a blue flower bowl at left and a small bronze statuette at right. Below, the centered title ROSALINDE and the line Robe du soir, de Worth.
images.caption: George Barbier, “Rosalinde. Robe du soir, de Worth”, Gazette du Bon Ton 1922, No. 10, plate 75. [Rijksmuseum](https://www.rijksmuseum.nl/en/collection/RP-P-2009-1964-4) RP-P-2009-1964-4, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gazette_du_Bon_Ton,_1922_-_No._10_Rosalinde_Robe_du_soir,_de_Worth,_RP-P-2009-1964-4.jpg).

rights.statement: The Rijksmuseum releases the scan under CC0 and marks the object “Publiek domein”. George Barbier died in 1932, and the plate was published in 1922.

references.title: “Victoire” car mascot by René Lalique
references.lede: René Lalique’s glass radiator mascot: a woman’s head whose hair streams back into a long fan of ribbed, clear glass, a symbol of speed.
references.summary: Frosted glass head with hair drawn back into a fan of parallel ribs. René Lalique, 1928.

source.label: Victoria and Albert Museum: Victoire, CIRC.199-1972

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected Morio’s 2013 photograph of the Toyota Automobile Museum example on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Victoire_2_by_Rene_Lalique_Toyota_Automobile_Museum.jpg) (3840 × 2880 px). Read the V&A record through its API and the Musée Lalique page with WebFetch.

styles.note: A canonical Art Deco luxury object: a machine-age speed motif rendered as stylized, repeated parallel ribs in pressed glass.

context: The Musée Lalique dates Victoire to 1928 and says Lalique made it to mark the tenth anniversary of the 1918 armistice, for the bonnets of luxury cars. It notes that glass mascots were phased out in the 1930s and reissued as statuettes on a base. [Musée Lalique](https://www.musee-lalique.com/en/exhibit-month/victoire-car-mascot/).

The V&A records the object as a radiator mascot, manufacturer’s title “Victoire”, popular title “Spirit of the Wind”, press-moulded glass, 15.5 × 25 × 6.5 cm, made ca. 1925 (range 1920–1935), for the Lalique glassworks at Wingen-sur-Moder. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O6383/victoire-radiator-mascot-lalique-rene-jules/).
observed: The head is in profile, with the mouth open and the eyes wide; the face and neck are frosted and smooth.
The hair sweeps back from the brow into a long, flat, rising fan of parallel ribs in clear glass that ends in a straight, slanted edge.
The ribs are close and regular and catch light as a series of bright lines.
The mascot sits on a short round frosted collar on a black display base.
Mold marks at the base are too faint in this photograph to read.
interpretation: The mascot turns speed into ornament: the wind is drawn as a regular fan of straight lines, the same radiating device the style uses for sunbursts.
It sits between core Art Deco and the later streamline branch: the subject is motion, but the form is still a stylized, symmetrical fan rather than a smooth teardrop.
borrow: Draw motion as a fan of evenly spaced straight lines behind a simple shape.
Pair a matte surface with glossy parallel ridges for contrast in one material.

images.alt: A frosted glass woman’s head in profile, mouth open, with hair streaming back into a long rising fan of clear ribbed glass, on a round base in a dark museum display case.
images.caption: René Lalique, “Victoire” car mascot, example in the Toyota Automobile Museum. Photograph by Morio, 2013, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Victoire_2_by_Rene_Lalique_Toyota_Automobile_Museum.jpg), CC BY-SA 3.0.

rights.statement: Photograph © Morio, [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/), via Wikimedia Commons. René Lalique died in 1945, so the design is in the public domain in France; it was issued before 1931, so it is also in the public domain in the United States.

references.title: Agay, PLM railway poster
references.lede: Roger Broders’s travel poster for the PLM railway frames a Riviera bay between pine trunks and sets the resort’s name in large geometric capitals.
references.summary: Flat blues, violets, and orange; bathers in cloche caps; the name AGAY in wide geometric capitals. Roger Broders, 1928.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the scan on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Roger_Broders_Agay_1928.jpg) (2100 × 2880 px), which Commons sources from the Bonhams lot photograph. Read the Bonhams lot page with WebFetch.

styles.note: A French railway travel poster of the late 1920s: flat stylized color, fashionable figures, and a heavy geometric capital title.

context: Bonhams catalogued the poster as “AGAY, PLM”, Roger Broders (1883–1953), 1928, lithographic poster in colours printed by Lucien Serre & Cie., Paris, 107 × 78.5 cm, in its 20th Century Decorative Arts & Design sale of 3 June 2021. [Bonhams](https://www.bonhams.com/auction/26798/lot/246/).

PLM is the Chemins de fer de Paris à Lyon et à la Méditerranée, whose monogram appears at the upper right. Commons files the poster under that company’s advertising posters. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Roger_Broders_Agay_1928.jpg).
observed: Tall pine trunks in orange and violet frame a view of a deep blue bay, a green headland, and a small lighthouse.
A woman in a black swimsuit and a red cloche cap stands in the foreground holding an orange wrap printed with dark flowers; a man sits at left.
Striped red-and-white parasols and small bathers dot the beach.
Color is laid in flat areas with little modelling: navy, violet, turquoise, orange, and cream.
“AGAY” is set very large in orange geometric sans-serif capitals with a dark outline and wide spacing, centered at the foot of the poster.
A second line in smaller orange capitals reads “PLAGE D’HIVER ET D’ÉTÉ - SUR LA CÔTE D’AZUR”. The PLM monogram sits in a gray block at upper right.
The landscape is asymmetrical and naturalistic in drawing; the geometry is in the lettering and the flat color.
interpretation: This is Art Deco as commercial travel imagery: the resort is sold through modern fashion, flat stylized color, and a monumental capital title, while the scene itself stays pictorial.
It is a weaker match than the architecture and furniture references for symmetry and ornament; it is here for its lettering and palette.
borrow: Set a short place name very large in geometric capitals with an outline, centered at the foot of the composition.
Use a deep violet or navy ground with one warm orange accent.

images.alt: Travel poster: a woman in a black swimsuit and red cap stands under tall orange and violet pine trees above a blue bay with striped parasols on the beach. At the bottom the word AGAY in large orange capitals, and the line Plage d'hiver et d'été, sur la Côte d'Azur.
images.caption: Roger Broders, “Agay”, poster for the PLM railway, 1928, printed by Lucien Serre & Cie. Image from the [Bonhams](https://www.bonhams.com/auction/26798/lot/246/) lot photograph, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Roger_Broders_Agay_1928.jpg).

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons marks the file public domain (PD-scan, PD-old-auto-expired, death year 1953). Roger Broders died in 1953, so the poster is public domain in France from 2024, and it was published in 1928, so it is public domain in the United States. The scan is a faithful reproduction of a two-dimensional work.

references.title: Akzidenz-Grotesk typeface
references.lede: A plain jobbing sans-serif from 1898 that Swiss designers of the 1950s made the voice of the style.
references.summary: Berthold’s 1898 grotesque; the preferred type of Swiss posters in the 1950s and 1960s.

creator.name: H. Berthold AG (Berthold Type Foundry), Berlin

evidence.note: Inspected the public-domain digital specimen [File:AkzidenzGroteskspecAIB1.svg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:AkzidenzGroteskspecAIB1.svg), rendered by Wikimedia at 960 px, and the 1905 Berthold advertisement [File:Berthold Sweden advertisement.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Berthold_Sweden_advertisement.jpg). Both are stored. The specimen shows a modern digital version, not the metal type.

styles.note: The style file names it first among the grotesques; Wikipedia records it as the preferred type of many Swiss designers in the 1950s and 1960s.

context: Akzidenz-Grotesk was released by the Berthold Type Foundry of Berlin in 1898. *Akzidenz* means jobbing work such as publicity, tickets, and forms. [Wikipedia: Akzidenz-Grotesk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akzidenz-Grotesk).

Wikipedia states that it was little known for about fifty years and then became the preferred typeface of many Swiss designers of the post-war International or Swiss style. It was sold as *Standard* in English-speaking countries. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akzidenz-Grotesk).

The 1905 advertisement shown here offers Royal-Grotesk, which Wikipedia says was later branded as the light weight of Akzidenz-Grotesk. It appeared in the Swedish printing journal *Almänna Svenska Boktryckareföreningens Meddelanden*. [Commons file page](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Berthold_Sweden_advertisement.jpg).

Josef Müller-Brockmann’s favourite typeface was Akzidenz-Grotesk, according to [Wikipedia: Josef Müller-Brockmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josef_M%C3%BCller-Brockmann). See [Der Film](ref:der-film-poster-1960) and [Neue Grafik](ref:neue-grafik-journal-1958-1965).
observed: Specimen: strokes are nearly even in weight, with no serifs and no visible contrast between thick and thin.
Specimen: terminals on a, e, and s are cut at an angle rather than horizontally; the R has a straight, diagonal leg.
Specimen: the regular and bold lines show the same letters, so the family reads as one voice in two weights.
1905 advertisement: the grotesque type sits in small, secondary lines (the agent’s name, the novelty lists) inside a heavy Jugendstil border of bars and squares, below a condensed display face.
interpretation: The 1905 advertisement shows the type before the style: the same neutral letters, but framed by ornament and centered. The International Typographic Style kept the letters and removed the frame.
Its value to Swiss designers was its ordinariness. A typeface made for tickets and forms carried no historical or artistic associations.
borrow: Choose a grotesque with slightly irregular, older proportions when a neo-grotesque feels too smooth. Use two weights of one family and let size do the rest.
Compare with [Helvetica](ref:helvetica-typeface) and [Univers](ref:univers-typeface), both developed in the 1950s from the same model.

images.alt: Type specimen of Akzidenz-Grotesk: the name in bold, “Aa Ee Rr” in regular and bold, a large white lowercase a, the word “Buchdruck” in red, and the lowercase alphabet and figures on a red band.
images.caption: Akzidenz-Grotesk specimen by GearedBull, 2006, released into the public domain. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:AkzidenzGroteskspecAIB1.svg), rendered from SVG to PNG by Wikimedia.

images.alt: A 1905 black-and-white advertisement for H. Berthold, Berlin, inside a heavy geometric border of bars and small squares. A condensed display face sets the firm’s name; plain grotesque type sets the Stockholm agent’s name and two lists of new typefaces.
images.caption: Berthold advertisement for its Swedish agent Fredr. Wagner, 1905, from *Almänna Svenska Boktryckareföreningens Meddelanden*. Public domain (published 1905). [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Berthold_Sweden_advertisement.jpg).

rights.statement: The specimen was released into the public domain by its author (PD-self, GearedBull) on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:AkzidenzGroteskspecAIB1.svg); letterform designs are not copyrightable in the United States. The 1905 advertisement is marked PD-1923 on [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Berthold_Sweden_advertisement.jpg). The Akzidenz-Grotesk name and font software belong to their owners.

references.title: Bacterio laminate, Abet Laminati product page
references.lede: The manufacturer’s current product page for Ettore Sottsass’s Bacterio laminate pattern.
references.summary: The Bacterio pattern in black on white: irregular squiggles and blobs at an even density.
references.made: Pattern 1978, per Abet’s and other sources; page current

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 25 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. A cookie consent panel covers the lower half of the screenshot. The pattern is visible.

references.title: Bauhaus building, Dessau
references.lede: Walter Gropius’s school building of 1925–26: separate volumes for each function, a glass curtain wall, and the school’s name in vertical sans-serif letters.
references.summary: White and gray volumes, a gridded glass curtain wall, and vertical BAUHAUS lettering. Walter Gropius, Dessau, 1926.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected two 1990 photographs by Sludge G on Wikimedia Commons ([workshop wing and lettering](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Das_Bauhaus,_Dessau,_DDR_May_1990_(5288787560).jpg), [entrance and bridge](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Das_Staatliche_Bauhaus,_Dessau,_DDR_May_1990_(5288786628).jpg)) and Lucia Moholy’s 1926 view from the northwest on the Bauhaus Kooperation page. None of the images is stored.

styles.note: The school’s own building: functional volumes, glass, steel, and white render, with Bauhaus lettering as part of the facade.

context: The building opened on 4 December 1926 with a two-day ceremony. Separate volumes hold the workshops, the technical school, the assembly hall and canteen, and the student studios; a bridge joins the workshop wing and the school. [Bauhaus Kooperation](https://bauhauskooperation.de/wissen/das-bauhaus/werke/architektur/bauhausgebaeude-dessau).

Bauhaus Kooperation notes the smooth white rendered facade and the materials reinforced concrete and glass. The building burned out in March 1945, has been a protected monument since 1972, and has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage site since 1996. [Bauhaus Kooperation](https://bauhauskooperation.de/wissen/das-bauhaus/werke/architektur/bauhausgebaeude-dessau).
Commons captions credit the facade lettering to Herbert Bayer. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Das_Bauhaus,_Dessau,_DDR_May_1990_(5288787560).jpg).
observed: The workshop wing is a three-storey box wrapped in a curtain wall of small, dark-framed glass panes that continues around the corner.
A white band of render forms the base of the glass wall; a recessed dark plinth sits below it.
A gray stair tower carries the word “BAUHAUS” in white sans-serif capitals, stacked vertically.
A two-storey bridge on concrete piers spans an open passage and joins two wings; its windows run in long horizontal bands.
In Lucia Moholy’s 1926 photograph the volumes are white, the glass is dark, and the building stands in open, unplanted ground.
Colors are neutral in the 1990 photographs; one yellow triangle appears only as a display behind a window.
interpretation: The building is Bauhaus architecture as a rubric: plain volumes, visible structure, glass as a surface, and type as part of the building. The palette is neutral, so the primary colors of the style belong to its graphics and interiors more than to its exterior.
The vertical lettering is an early example of architectural signage that uses the same sans-serif language as the school’s print work.
borrow: Give each function its own clear volume or panel, and show the joins between them.
Use a fine, regular grid of thin dark lines over a large area, as in the curtain wall, to add texture without ornament.
Stack a short word vertically in sans-serif capitals as a sign.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Commons photographs are CC BY-SA 2.0, but the building is by Walter Gropius, who died in 1969, so it is protected in Germany until 2039. German freedom of panorama (§ 59 UrhG) and the United States exclusion of pre-1990 buildings would probably permit exterior photographs; the lead curator can decide whether to upgrade to tier A. Lucia Moholy’s 1926 photograph is © VG Bild-Kunst per Bauhaus Kooperation.

references.title: Bauhaus signet
references.lede: Oskar Schlemmer’s profile of a head, built only from rectangles and bars inside a circle, became the school’s mark from 1922.
references.summary: A face in profile made of white rectangles and bars inside a circle. Oskar Schlemmer, 1922.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the PNG rendering of the [Commons vector file](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bauhaus-Signet.svg). The file is a modern vector redrawing of the signet, not a scan of a 1922 print.

styles.note: The school’s own mark: a figure reduced to orthogonal bars and blocks inside a circle.

context: Commons describes the file as the signet of the Staatliches Bauhaus, designed by Oskar Schlemmer and used from 1922, and cites Hans M. Wingler, Bauhaus: Weimar, Dessau, Berlin, Chicago (MIT Press, 1969). [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bauhaus-Signet.svg).

The 1923 exhibition competition required the signet, and Joost Schmidt’s poster includes it. [Bauhaus Kooperation](https://bauhauskooperation.de/wissen/das-bauhaus/werke/graphische-druckerei/plakat-zur-bauhaus-ausstellung-in-weimar-1923). See [the poster](ref:bauhaus-exhibition-poster-1923).
observed: A thin white circle frames a black disc on a black square.
A long vertical white bar divides the disc slightly right of center.
White rectangles and thin bars at left of the bar suggest an eye, a nose, a mouth, and a neck in profile.
All parts except the circle are horizontal or vertical; there are no diagonals or curves inside the face.
interpretation: The signet shows the Bauhaus idea of the human figure as a constructed system. It is the reverse of an ornamental emblem: the face is only a set of blocks.
Because it uses only black and white, it shows that the style depends on elementary shapes as much as on primary color.
borrow: Draw an icon or figure only from rectangles and one enclosing circle.
Use one strong vertical bar as the axis of a mark.

images.alt: Black disc in a thin white circle; a vertical white bar and white rectangles and bars form a stylized face in profile facing left.
images.caption: Bauhaus signet by Oskar Schlemmer, 1922, vector redrawing on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bauhaus-Signet.svg), rendered to PNG by Wikimedia. Public domain.

rights.statement: Marked public domain on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bauhaus-Signet.svg). Schlemmer died in 1943. The vector file is a redrawing derived from an earlier Commons image by Hendrike.

references.title: Bauhaus table lamp (Wagenfeld and Jucker)
references.lede: The “Bauhaus lamp”: an opal glass hemisphere on a straight shaft over a round base, all parts plain geometric solids.
references.summary: Opal glass dome, clear or metal shaft, disc base. Wilhelm Wagenfeld and Carl Jakob Jucker, Bauhaus metal workshop, 1923–24.

creator.name: Wilhelm Wagenfeld and Carl Jakob Jucker

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected, in the scratchpad only, the metal version photographed by Joachim Fliegner on the Bauhaus Kooperation page and a [Commons photograph by Sailko](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tischlampe_di_Carl_Jakob_Jucker_(left,_1923-24)_e_di_Wilhelm_Wagenfeld_(right,_1924)_(cropped).JPG) of the glass-base version at Weimar.

styles.note: A canonical Bauhaus product: a hemisphere, a cylinder, and a disc, with visible fittings.

context: Bauhaus Kooperation says Wagenfeld made the lamp in 1924, planned it as a general-purpose lamp for living rooms, and followed the geometric rules of his teacher László Moholy-Nagy. [Bauhaus Kooperation](https://bauhauskooperation.de/wissen/das-bauhaus/werke/metall/bauhaus-leuchte).
MoMA credits Wilhelm Wagenfeld and Carl Jakob Jucker, 1923–1924. [MoMA 4056](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/4056).
observed: A white opal glass shade is close to a hemisphere and sits on a thin flat metal ring.
A threaded metal collar with a pull switch joins the shade to a straight cylindrical shaft.
One version has a clear glass shaft and a thick clear glass disc base, with the wire visible inside the shaft.
The other version has a polished metal shaft and a flat metal disc base on small ball feet.
The pull chain ends in a small metal ball.
interpretation: The lamp is the object form of the style’s shape vocabulary. The glass version also shows “honest materials”: the wire and fittings stay visible.
borrow: Combine one hemisphere, one cylinder, and one disc; do not add transitions or decoration.
Leave functional parts, such as a switch or cable, visible and neat.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Bauhaus Kooperation credits its photograph “Wilhelm Wagenfeld Stiftung, Bremen / © VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn.” The Commons photograph is CC BY-SA 3.0, but the lamp design is still protected; Wagenfeld died in 1990.

references.title: Bauhaus100 centenary website, 2019
references.lede: The official website of the Bauhaus centenary year, as archived in February 2019.
references.summary: A revival identity: slate-blue field, a lowercase “100 jahre bauhaus” mark, yellow headline, red map.

evidence.note: Captured from the Internet Archive with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 25 September 2026 and inspected. The archived page may lack some images or scripts that the live page had. A cookie bar appears at the bottom.

styles.note: A 2019 web revival. It passes the fingerprint, measured on screenshot pixels for hue count.

observed: A flat slate-blue field fills the page behind the content.
The logo is a blocky yellow 100 above lowercase “jahre bauhaus” in a geometric sans-serif.
The headline is set in heavy yellow sans-serif. A flat yellow button carries black text.
The slide image is a map of Germany with one state in flat red.
Navigation is white sans-serif. Slider arrows and dots are plain white.
interpretation: The revival keeps the lowercase logotype, flat primary accents, and heavy sans-serif, but places them on a muted blue-gray instead of paper white. That muted ground is a 2010s choice, not a Bauhaus one.

references.title: Bauhausbücher 8: Malerei, Fotografie, Film
references.lede: Moholy-Nagy’s own volume in the Bauhaus book series, with a cover that sets red sans-serif type over a close-up photograph of a camera.
references.summary: Red and white sans-serif type over a black-and-white photograph. László Moholy-Nagy, Bauhausbücher 8, second edition, 1927.

source.label: MoMA: Bauhausbücher 8, L. Moholy-Nagy: Malerei, Fotografie, Film

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the [Commons scan of the 1927 cover](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bauhausb%C3%BCcher_8,_Malerei,_Fotografie,_Film.jpg) (1612 × 2000 px). Also compared the [1925 first-edition cover](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:L%C3%A1szl%C3%B3_Moholy-Nagy_Malerei_Umschlag_1925.jpg), which spells “Photographie”.

styles.note: Bauhaus typophoto: geometric sans-serif type in red, white, and black laid over photography, from the school’s own book series.

context: MoMA catalogues the cover as “Bauhausbücher 8, L. Moholy-Nagy: Malerei, Fotografie, Film,” 1927. [MoMA 8089](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/8089). The Commons file cites this MoMA record as its source and describes the image as the second edition of 1927. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bauhausb%C3%BCcher_8,_Malerei,_Fotografie,_Film.jpg).

The Bauhaus published the Bauhausbücher from 1925 to 1930 with Albert Langen Verlag; Walter Gropius and László Moholy-Nagy were the editors. [Wikipedia (de): Bauhausbücher](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bauhausb%C3%BCcher).

The first edition appeared in 1925 with the spelling “Photographie” on the cover. [Commons, 1925 cover](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:L%C3%A1szl%C3%B3_Moholy-Nagy_Malerei_Umschlag_1925.jpg).
observed: A dark, grainy close-up photograph of a camera or projector fills the cover; one round lens with two bright highlights is at upper left.
“BAUHAUS BÜCHER” runs across the top in red geometric sans-serif capitals.
A large red numeral 8 sits inside the lens ring.
The author name is in white capitals; “MALEREI” and “FILM” are in red, “FOTOGRAFIE” in white, all flush left.
The scanned paper has torn and worn edges.
interpretation: The cover shows the Bauhaus interest in machines and new media. The photograph replaces drawn geometry, but the circle of the lens still works as an elementary shape.
The red-white-black scheme and flush-left sans-serif stack became a template for later modernist book design.
borrow: Put one strong numeral inside a circular form in a photograph to tie type to image.
Alternate two colors line by line in a flush-left title stack.

images.alt: Book cover: a dark photograph of a camera lens with a large red numeral 8 inside the lens ring; red capitals read Bauhaus Bücher at the top, and L. Moholy-Nagy, Malerei, Fotografie, Film are stacked flush left in white and red at the bottom.
images.caption: László Moholy-Nagy, cover of Bauhausbücher 8, second edition, 1927. Scan on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bauhausb%C3%BCcher_8,_Malerei,_Fotografie,_Film.jpg), public domain.

rights.statement: Marked public domain on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bauhausb%C3%BCcher_8,_Malerei,_Fotografie,_Film.jpg). Moholy-Nagy died in 1946, and this edition was published in 1927. The scan is a faithful reproduction of a two-dimensional work.

references.title: Bel Air chair
references.lede: Peter Shire’s armchair for Memphis: a fin-shaped back, a bolster arm, and a ball for a foot.
references.summary: Peter Shire’s 1982 Memphis armchair of colored blocks, a cylinder, and a sphere.

evidence.note: Downloaded the museum’s published image (843 px wide) from [the V&A IIIF server](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1175028/) to a private scratchpad and inspected it with the Read tool on 2026-09-25. No image is stored in the catalogue.

styles.note: The V&A calls it a signature object of the Memphis collective.

context: The V&A calls the Bel Air the most important contribution of the Californian designer Peter Shire to Memphis. It was on the cover of Barbara Radice’s widely distributed book on the group and, as a cartoon, on material for the exhibition “Memphis in Memphis” (Memphis Brooks Museum of Art, 1984/85). [V&A record](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1175028/).

The record says the asymmetrical back refers to shark fins and to John Lautner’s Stevens House in Malibu, and that the name comes from a Beverly Hills hotel, like other early Memphis titles. The V&A example has the original colors. [V&A record](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1175028/).
Materials: painted wood and colored cotton fabric. [V&A record](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1175028/).
observed: The back is a tall quarter-circle in deep crimson, rising higher on one side than the other.
A lime-green cylinder lies across one arm, and an orange sphere supports the opposite rear corner.
The seat cushion is pale mint, the side panel is beige, and the plinth is a pale blue-green block.
Each part is a different solid color with no pattern.
interpretation: The chair is assembled from primitive solids, a quarter-disc, a cylinder, a sphere, and blocks, each in its own color. This is the toy geometry of Memphis in upholstered form.
borrow: Build a shape from a few primitive solids and color each one differently.
Break symmetry with one oversized element, such as a quarter-circle or a sphere placed off-axis.

rights.statement: The V&A image is credited © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. No image is stored.

references.title: Bliss
references.lede: Charles O’Rear’s green hill under a blue sky: the Windows XP wallpaper that made saturated nature the default view of a computer.
references.summary: Green hill, blue sky, white clouds. Photograph 1996, Windows XP default wallpaper 2001.

evidence.note: Inspected the non-free 365 × 274 reduction [File:Bliss (Windows XP).png](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bliss_(Windows_XP).png) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Avcı traces the style’s nature imagery partly to Bliss, and Wikipedia lists it under “See also”; it is a precursor from the Windows XP era.

context: Bliss, originally titled Bucolic Green Hills, was photographed by Charles O’Rear in January 1996 near the Napa–Sonoma county line, California, on Fujifilm Velvia. Microsoft obtained full rights in 2000 and used it as the Windows XP default wallpaper. [Wikipedia: Bliss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bliss_(photograph)).

Avcı links the style’s nature visuals to HD-television demonstration imagery and to “the iconic ‘Bliss’ desktop wallpaper,” which “inspired many brands.” [Avcı 2024, “Physical reflections of digital aesthetics”](https://doi.org/10.17932/IAU.EJNM.25480200.2024/ejnm_v8i3003), p. 472.
observed: A smooth, bright green hill fills the lower half; the grass is saturated and almost uniform.
The sky is a clear, deep blue that lightens toward the horizon.
Soft white cumulus and thin cirrus clouds cross the sky; distant hills sit low at the right.
interpretation: Bliss has no gloss and no interface, so it is not Frutiger Aero by itself. It is the nature half of the style in its plainest form: technology presented through a clean, saturated, human-free landscape.
borrow: Use a real, very saturated sky-and-grass photograph as a calm backdrop behind glass panels, with no people in it.

rights.statement: Copyrighted photograph; rights held by Microsoft per Wikipedia. No image is stored here.

references.title: BoldKit website
references.lede: The site of a neubrutalism component library for React and Vue, with a live component preview in the hero.
references.summary: Condensed display type, outlined tags and buttons with hard shadows, and a pastel grid ground.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 25 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Passes the fingerprint: 2 px outlines on 91% of boxes, hard shadows, square corners, and five hues of strong accents.

observed: The wordmark BOLD KIT is set very large in a condensed sans-serif, with KIT in outline letters.
Framework tags (React, Vue 3, Nuxt, MCP) are small outlined labels in flat colors with hard shadows.
A coral Get Started button and white Browse Components and GitHub buttons all have black outlines and hard shadows.
A preview panel with a black frame shows outlined buttons, shape tiles, and stat cards.
The page ground is off-white with a faint grid. Body text is monospaced.
interpretation: Adds monospaced body text and condensed display type to the grammar. This is where neo-brutalism touches the technical, instrument-like side of [Minimalist Machine](style:minimalist-machine).

references.title: Boudoir of the Hôtel du Collectionneur, Paris 1925
references.lede: An autochrome taken at the 1925 Paris exhibition: Ruhlmann’s boudoir in the Pavillon du Collectionneur, with gilded panels, a basket of gold disks over the mirror, and dark lacquered furniture.
references.summary: Pale paneling with gilt fillets, a gilded disk ornament, paired sconces, and black furniture. Ruhlmann pavilion, Paris, 1925.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: musée départemental Albert-Kahn, A46733S

creator.name: Émile-Jacques Ruhlmann (ensemble); photograph by Léon Auguste for the Archives de la Planète

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the musée Albert-Kahn autochrome from Wikimedia Commons (1520 × 2048 px). The museum’s own notice page returned HTTP 403 to a script and to Claude in Chrome, so the metadata comes from the Commons record, which copies it.

styles.note: A room from the pavilion that the 1925 Exposition made the showpiece of French luxury Art Deco, recorded in color in the year of the exhibition.

references.notice: The musée Albert-Kahn notice page could not be opened on 2026-09-25 (HTTP 403). Rights and metadata are taken from the Commons copy.
context: Commons records the autochrome as A46733S of the musée départemental Albert-Kahn, operator Léon Auguste, mission “1925 – Exposition internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels modernes Paris”, dated 15 September 1925. The original caption reads “Petit Salon du Pavon Rhulmann”. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:L%27Exposition_des_arts_d%C3%A9coratifs,_Pavillon_Ruhlmann_ou_H%C3%B4tel_d%27un_Riche_Collectionneur,_boudoir_-_A46733S.jpg).
The style this room belongs to takes its name from the 1925 Exposition. See [Art Deco](style:art-deco).
observed: The room is pale gray-white with thin gilt fillets that divide the walls into tall vertical panels.
A gilded relief of overlapping disks in a fluted basket sits above a tall rectangular mirror with a gilt frame.
Two gilt wall sconces with pleated shades flank the mirror symmetrically.
A cylindrical crystal chandelier of stacked tiers hangs from a cornice with a gilded dentil band.
A black lacquered writing desk with a curved roll top and a black chair stand at lower left; an armchair covered in pale fabric with a dark frame stands beside them.
A round screen in front of the fireplace shows dark birds with spread wings in a radiating arrangement.
Green silk curtains hang at the left window. A small bronze figure and a framed portrait photograph stand on the mantelpiece.
The colors are soft and grainy, as is usual for an autochrome.
interpretation: The room is the ensemblier idea in one view: furniture, wall panels, lighting, and ornament are designed together around one symmetrical axis through the mantel and mirror.
The gilded basket of disks is a stylized bouquet, the same motif as the inlay on Ruhlmann’s [corner cabinet](ref:ruhlmann-corner-cabinet-1923), turned into flat circles.
borrow: Divide a pale ground into tall panels with thin gold rules.
Place one gilded ornament on the central axis and pair identical elements on each side of it.
Set black, glossy objects against a pale room for contrast instead of using a dark ground everywhere.

images.alt: Color autochrome of a pale paneled boudoir. Above a white mantelpiece, a gilt-framed mirror is flanked by two gilt sconces and topped by a gilded relief of stacked disks. A crystal chandelier hangs above; a black roll-top desk, a black chair, and a pale armchair stand in front, beside green curtains.
images.caption: Léon Auguste, boudoir of the Pavillon Ruhlmann (Hôtel du Collectionneur), Exposition des arts décoratifs, Paris, 15 September 1925. Autochrome, musée départemental Albert-Kahn A46733S, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:L%27Exposition_des_arts_d%C3%A9coratifs,_Pavillon_Ruhlmann_ou_H%C3%B4tel_d%27un_Riche_Collectionneur,_boudoir_-_A46733S.jpg).

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons marks the file CC0 as a musée départemental Albert-Kahn upload. The room is Ruhlmann’s (died 1933). The small bronze figure, the portrait photograph, and the painted fire screen are by unidentified makers and appear incidentally; the lead curator should confirm that this is acceptable.

references.title: Brutalist Websites
references.lede: Pascal Deville’s directory of raw websites: the ancestor that lent neo-brutalism its name, not an example of it.
references.summary: Lineage reference: the brutalist web directory that preceded the colorful neo-brutalist style.

evidence.note: Live home page captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) and inspected on 25 September 2026. The 2014 start date and Deville’s authorship come from secondary sources.

styles.note: Lineage only: it is the brutalist web design that neo-brutalism descends from and must be distinguished from.

references.notice: This is a lineage reference. Brutalist web design is raw and often default-styled. Neo-brutalism is a polished, colorful component system with thick outlines and hard shadows. Do not use this site as evidence of neo-brutalist traits.
context: The site’s tagline reads: “In its ruggedness and lack of concern to look comfortable or easy, Brutalism can be seen as a reaction by a younger generation to the lightness, optimism, and frivolity of today's web design.”
The [Webflow blog](https://webflow.com/blog/10-brutalist-websites) and other secondary sources credit Pascal Deville with launching it in 2014.

[Michał Malewicz, “Neubrutalism is taking over the web” (Hype4 Academy, first published 28 March 2022)](https://hype4.academy/articles/design/neubrutalism-is-taking-over-web) describes neubrutalism as brutalism in web design mixed with modern typography, illustration, and animation. [NN/g, “Neobrutalism: Definition and Best Practices” (Hayat Sheikh, 11 April 2025)](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/neobrutalism/) contrasts brutalist sites with more colorful and orderly neobrutalist ones.
interpretation: Keep it beside the neo-brutalist records to show the break: the name and the anti-polish attitude carried over, but the visual system did not. The measurement confirms this: zero outlines and zero shadows.

rights.statement: The directory and the listed sites belong to their owners. Screenshot captured for commentary.

observed: A light gray page with a short monospaced introduction at top left and a Submit link.
Submitted sites appear as a loose grid of screenshots with monospaced captions.
No component has an outline, shadow, or rounded corner. The only strong colors come from the screenshots.

images.alt: Brutalist Websites home page: a gray page with a short monospaced text block at top left and a loose grid of website screenshots with monospaced captions, including RAW Magazine, Disslist, and Nelson Heinemann.
images.caption: First viewport of [brutalistwebsites.com](https://brutalistwebsites.com/).

references.title: Carlton room divider
references.lede: Ettore Sottsass’s laminate bookcase from the first Memphis collection: a totem of tilted shelves in a dozen flat colors.
references.summary: Sottsass’s 1981 laminate bookcase: angled shelves, many colors, a speckled base.

source.label: Art Institute of Chicago: Carlton Room Divider (1984.1035)

creator.name: Ettore Sottsass, Jr.; Memphis Furniture, S.R.L.

evidence.note: Downloaded the museum’s published image (843 px wide) from [the Art Institute of Chicago IIIF server](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/103026) to a private scratchpad and inspected it with the Read tool on 2026-09-25. No image is stored in the catalogue. The Met holds a second example; its record was read but shows no image.

styles.note: A founding piece of the 1981 Memphis collection and the group’s best-known object.

context: The Art Institute describes the Carlton as a bookshelf and cabinet from the 1981 Memphis launch, made of wood and colored plastic laminate, 194.3 × 189.8 × 40 cm. [AIC record](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/103026).

The same record says the tiered form recalls “the head and arms of an ancient idol or totem” and links it to Sottsass’s laminate Superboxes of the 1960s for Poltronova. [AIC record](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/103026).
The Met holds another example, accession 1997.460.1a–d, dated 1981, wood and plastic laminate. [Met record](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/486989).
observed: Shelves slant outward at about 45 degrees on each side, so the silhouette is a symmetrical fan of diagonals rather than a grid.
Each shelf and support has its own flat color: green, pale yellow, pink, light blue, red, dark blue, orange, black, gray, and brown.
A small red two-drawer cabinet sits at the center, under a pink triangle and a yellow tray topped by an empty square frame.
Small black triangles fill the joints where diagonal shelves meet horizontal ones.
The plinth is covered in a white laminate with dense black squiggle marks.
interpretation: The Carlton shows the Memphis method in one object: a useful bookcase is broken into parts, and each part gets a different color, so the object reads as a figure or a toy before it reads as storage.
The patterned base against the flat-colored shelves is the style’s pairing of printed surface and solid color.
borrow: Give each structural part its own flat color and let diagonals carry the composition.
Put a busy black-and-white pattern on one base element as a foil for the solid colors above it.

rights.statement: AIC marks the object as not public domain, © 2018 Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York / ADAGP, Paris. No image is stored.

references.title: Casablanca sideboard
references.lede: A sideboard from the first Memphis collection, covered entirely in sponge-patterned laminate.
references.summary: Sottsass’s 1981 sideboard: a central column with angled arms in speckled red laminate.

evidence.note: Downloaded the museum’s published image (843 px wide) from [the V&A IIIF server](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O58652/) to a private scratchpad and inspected it with the Read tool on 2026-09-25. No image is stored in the catalogue.

styles.note: Part of the first Memphis collection; its patterned laminate is a direct example of the style’s surface grammar.

context: The V&A says the sideboard was part of the first Memphis furniture collection, made of plastic laminate over fibreboard. Sottsass designed it for storage and display and as a room divider; the angled arms are meant to hold wine bottles. [V&A record](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O58652/).

The V&A links the laminate to American diner interiors and 1950s kitchen furniture, and notes that the furniture was too expensive for the average customer despite its “low taste” sources. [V&A record](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O58652/).
The physical description names a sponged pattern in red, black, white, and yellow. [V&A record](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O58652/).
observed: A central column carries a tall gray-and-white mottled door panel, a yellow-and-black mottled drawer, and a solid black lower section.
Red shelves with black speckles branch from the column: angled arms at the top, long diagonal arms at the sides, and V-shaped cradles lower down.
Every visible surface except the black base carries a mottled, sponge-like print.
The outline is symmetrical and reads as a figure with raised arms.
interpretation: Where the [Carlton](ref:sottsass-carlton-room-divider-1981) uses many flat colors, the Casablanca uses three patterned laminates. Both show that Memphis pattern is applied to whole surfaces, not used as trim.
borrow: Cover whole panels in one coarse mottled texture and change the color from panel to panel.
Use a symmetrical, figure-like outline with diagonal arms to make a practical object look like a character.

rights.statement: The V&A image is credited © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. No image is stored.

references.title: Chrysler Building, New York
references.lede: William Van Alen’s skyscraper, completed in 1930: a setback tower capped by a stainless-steel crown of stacked, radiating arches and a needle spire.
references.summary: Stepped setbacks and a steel crown of radiating arches with triangular windows. William Van Alen, New York, 1930.

source.label: Library of Congress: Empire State Building, New York City. [View from], to Chrysler Bldg. and Queensboro Bridge

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected Samuel H. Gottscho’s photograph of 19 January 1932 from the Library of Congress via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Chrysler_Building_Midtown_Manhattan_New_York_City_1932.jpg) (5359 × 3779 px, grayscale). The photograph is an aerial view from the Empire State Building, so the crown is legible but small; street-level ornament such as the eagle and hubcap details is not visible.

styles.note: The canonical Art Deco skyscraper: tiered setbacks rise to a crown of radiating, stepped arches in polished metal.

context: Construction started on 21 January 1929, the spire was installed on 23 October 1929, and the building opened on 27 May 1930. It was the tallest building in the world for about 11 months. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysler_Building).

Wikipedia describes the crown as seven radiating terraced arches clad in Nirosta stainless steel, with triangular vaulted windows, and notes car-hood ornaments on the 31st floor and eagle gargoyles on the 61st. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysler_Building).
The Library of Congress dates the photograph 19 January 1932 and credits the Gottscho-Schleisner Collection (LC-DIG-ppmsca-05841). [Library of Congress](https://www.loc.gov/item/2018751223/).
observed: The tower rises from the center of the frame above lower Midtown blocks; its outline steps in at several setbacks before the crown.
The crown is a stack of diminishing arches, each pierced by a row of small triangular windows that fan out like rays.
A thin needle spire continues the central axis above the arches.
The crown reflects light more strongly than the brick shaft below it.
Neighboring towers also step back in tiers; the photograph shows the setback silhouette as a citywide pattern.
The photograph is black and white, so the color of the steel and brick is not recorded.
interpretation: The crown is the sunburst motif of the style built at city scale: nested arches radiate from one axis and diminish toward a point.
The tiered setbacks are the architectural source of the stepped frames and ziggurat outlines that appear in Deco graphics and furniture.
borrow: Build a heading or hero ornament from nested arches that shrink toward one central point.
Step the outline of a frame or card inward in two or three tiers instead of rounding its corners.

images.alt: Black-and-white aerial photograph of Midtown Manhattan in 1932. The Chrysler Building stands at the center, its tower stepping back to a pointed crown of stacked arches with small triangular windows and a needle spire. The East River and Queensboro Bridge lie behind.
images.caption: Samuel H. Gottscho, view from the Empire State Building to the Chrysler Building and Queensboro Bridge, 19 January 1932. Gottscho-Schleisner Collection, [Library of Congress](https://www.loc.gov/item/2018751223/), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Chrysler_Building_Midtown_Manhattan_New_York_City_1932.jpg).

rights.statement: The Library of Congress states “No known restrictions on publication” for this Gottscho-Schleisner photograph; Wikimedia Commons marks the file public domain. The building was completed in 1930, before United States copyright protected architectural works (1990), and William Van Alen died in 1954.
