references.title: Cobra lamp by Edgar Brandt
references.lede: Edgar Brandt’s bronze floor lamp: a cobra coils up a thin stem and holds a conical glass shade in its body, its hood raised beside the rim.
references.summary: A bronze cobra twined around a stem holding a conical amber glass shade. Edgar Brandt with Daum, c. 1925.

source.label: Art Institute of Chicago: Cobra Lamp, 1984.73

creator.name: Edgar William Brandt; glass attributed to Daum Frères

evidence.note: Downloaded the Art Institute of Chicago IIIF image (843 × 1393 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. Read the record through the AIC API. No image is stored.

styles.note: The Art Institute classifies it as Art Deco. It shows the luxury metalwork of the 1925 generation and the taste for exotic, stylized animals.

context: The Art Institute records the lamp as c. 1925, bronze and glass, height 91.8 cm, by Edgar William Brandt (French, 1880–1960), with glass attributed to Daum Frères, Nancy, and metalwork attributed to Mueller Frères, Lunéville. Style: Art Deco. [Art Institute of Chicago](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/109535/cobra-lamp).
The AIC API marks the object as not in the public domain (`is_public_domain: false`). [AIC API](https://api.artic.edu/api/v1/artworks/109535).
observed: A dark bronze cobra forms the whole lamp: its tail coils flat on a round ribbed base, its body rises as a thin stem, wraps once around the bottom of the shade, and lifts its hooded head beside the rim.
The scales are cast as a fine diamond crosshatch along the body.
The shade is a tall inverted cone of mottled amber glass, pale green inside.
The lamp is tall and slender; the only curved lines are in the snake.
interpretation: The lamp shows the exotic, animal side of Art Deco, influenced by the fashion for Egypt and the Orient; it is less geometric than the architectural references.
The contrast of dark patinated metal with warm glass is the material palette of luxury Deco lighting.
borrow: Pair one dark metal color with one warm translucent color.
Use a single stylized animal as the structural element instead of as applied decoration.

rights.statement: The Art Institute does not mark the image public domain. Edgar Brandt died in 1960, so the design is protected in France until 2030.

references.title: Corner cabinet by Émile-Jacques Ruhlmann
references.lede: A tall corner cabinet in dark exotic wood whose door carries an oval of ivory marquetry: a ribbed vase in a dense wreath of stylized flowers.
references.summary: Dark wood, ivory inlay, a stylized flower basket in an oval, and tapered legs with ivory feet. Ruhlmann, Paris, c. 1923.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Brooklyn Museum photograph published on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Emile-Jacques_Ruhlmann_(French,_1879-1933)._Corner_Cabinet,_ca._1923..jpg) (1214 × 1536 px), a frontal studio view on a gray ground. Read the museum record in Claude in Chrome.

styles.note: A key work of the ensemblier who defined French Art Deco luxury furniture: rare dark wood, ivory, and a symmetrical, stylized floral ornament.

context: The Brooklyn Museum dates the cabinet c. 1923, gives its place of making as Paris, and lists mahogany, Macassar ebony, rosewood, ebony, ivory, amaranth, and brass. It is branded “RUHLMANN” twice on the back panels. [Brooklyn Museum](https://www.brooklynmuseum.org/opencollection/objects/97886).

The Commons caption from the museum’s 2014 upload gives the materials as kingwood (amaranth) veneer on mahogany with ivory inlay, and the size as 126.7 × 80.6 × 59.7 cm. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Emile-Jacques_Ruhlmann_(French,_1879-1933)._Corner_Cabinet,_ca._1923..jpg).

Search-result text from the museum’s catalogue says Ruhlmann designed the cabinet for “Les Terrasses,” the house of A. Weitz in Lyon, and links the black-and-white inlay to the Wiener Werkstätte. This was not shown on the page text read on 2026-09-25. [Brooklyn Museum](https://www.brooklynmuseum.org/opencollection/objects/97886).
observed: The front is a single door of red-brown wood with a slightly bowed outline, framed by a line of small ivory dots.

An upright oval of ivory marquetry fills most of the door. In it a dark, fluted vase with ivory rib lines and scrolled handles holds a dense mass of stylized flowers and leaves in ivory and dark wood.
The composition is symmetrical about the vertical axis of the door.
The top edge carries a band of alternating ivory and dark blocks, like a dentil or piano-key border.
Three slender, tapered legs end in small ivory sabots; two ivory disks mark the tops of the front legs.
There is no metal mount on the front except a small keyhole escutcheon.
interpretation: The piece shows the early, luxurious side of Art Deco: an eighteenth-century furniture type made new with flattened, geometric flower ornament and a strong dark-and-ivory contrast.
The basket of stylized flowers is a stock motif of 1920s French decorative art, here held inside a strict oval and a symmetrical axis.
borrow: Frame a central ornament with a single row of small dots in the accent color.
Use one strong light-on-dark ornament, centered, on an otherwise plain surface.
Edge a panel with a band of alternating light and dark blocks.

images.alt: Studio photograph of a tall corner cabinet in reddish-brown wood on three slender tapered legs with ivory feet. Its door has an oval of ivory inlay showing a dark ribbed vase overflowing with stylized white flowers, framed by a line of small ivory dots.
images.caption: Émile-Jacques Ruhlmann, corner cabinet, c. 1923. [Brooklyn Museum](https://www.brooklynmuseum.org/opencollection/objects/97886) 71.150.1, photograph by the Brooklyn Museum via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Emile-Jacques_Ruhlmann_(French,_1879-1933)._Corner_Cabinet,_ca._1923..jpg).

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons carries the Brooklyn Museum’s “No known copyright restrictions” statement for this photograph. Ruhlmann died in 1933, so the design is in the public domain in France and the United States. The museum’s own object page offers the image for download but shows no license text.

references.title: Crystal Clear icons
references.lede: Everaldo Coelho’s glossy, translucent desktop icons: saturated color, bright highlights, and soft shading.
references.summary: Glossy, gel-like 3D icons in saturated colors. Everaldo Coelho for KDE and Linux desktops.

evidence.note: Inspected the 128 × 128 LGPL icon [File:Crystal Clear kdmconfig-danger.png](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Crystal_Clear_kdmconfig-danger.png) and stored it.

styles.note: Wikipedia uses this icon to illustrate the style’s vibrant colors, three-dimensional graphics, and glossy textures.

context: Coelho’s “crystal” look “consists of icons that appear to be made of highly reflective surfaces.” He aimed “between realism of Mac OS X and cartoon colored style of XP.” Crystal SVG became KDE’s default icon theme in KDE 3.1; the later Crystal Clear set made icons appear transparent. [Wikipedia: Everaldo Coelho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everaldo_Coelho).

The Wikipedia Frutiger Aero article illustrates “vibrant colors, three-dimensional graphics, and glossy textures” with this icon, and lists Crystal icons under “See also.” [Wikipedia: Frutiger Aero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frutiger_Aero).
observed: Three rounded, faceless figures in saturated green, blue, and red look like molded gel.
Each figure has a bright white specular highlight on the head and shoulder and darker shading at the edges.
A yellow warning triangle with an exclamation mark overlaps the front, with a soft shadow.
interpretation: Crystal predates Vista, but it already has the style’s icon grammar: candy color, gel volume, and a single hard highlight. It helped make gloss the default look of free desktops.
borrow: Draw icons as simple rounded volumes with one strong white highlight and a darker rim, rather than outlines.

images.alt: Glossy icon of three rounded human figures in green, blue, and red with white highlights, and a yellow warning triangle with an exclamation mark.
images.caption: Crystal Clear “kdmconfig-danger” icon by Everaldo Coelho (YellowIcon). LGPL. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Crystal_Clear_kdmconfig-danger.png).

rights.statement: “All Crystal icons were posted by the author as LGPL on kde-look” ([Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Crystal_Clear_kdmconfig-danger.png)). Credit: Everaldo Coelho (YellowIcon).

references.title: Der Film exhibition poster
references.lede: Josef Müller-Brockmann’s all-type poster for a film exhibition: the title slides across the sheet like a moving credit.
references.summary: Josef Müller-Brockmann, 1960. Akzidenz-Grotesk overlapping on black, with red text on one axis.

source.label: eMuseum, Museum für Gestaltung Zürich: poster M-0314

evidence.note: Downloaded the scan at [File:Josef Müller-Brockmann der Film.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Josef_M%C3%BCller-Brockmann_der_Film.jpg) (1423 × 2000 px, sourced by the uploader from MoMA) to a scratch folder and inspected it. Catalogue data read on the eMuseum, MoMA, and Library of Congress records. The image is not stored.

styles.note: A purely typographic poster by a Neue Grafik editor: one grotesque, flush-left text on a single axis, and extreme scale contrast.

context: Poster for the exhibition *Der Film* at the Kunstgewerbemuseum Zürich, 1960. Offset, 127 × 90 cm, printed by Graphische Anstalt J. E. Wolfensberger AG, Zürich. Object M-0314, Plakatsammlung. [eMuseum, Museum für Gestaltung Zürich](https://www.emuseum.ch/objects/65641).

MoMA holds a copy: offset lithograph, 90.1 × 127.6 cm, gift of the Kunstgewerbemuseum Zürich, object 57.1960. [MoMA](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/4882). The Library of Congress holds another (POS - Switz .M65, no. 5). [LoC](https://www.loc.gov/item/2004675046/).

Fonts In Use, citing the museum’s eGuide, reports that the title was set in Akzidenz-Grotesk, exposed on photographic paper at several positions and degrees of sharpness, and retouched with opaque white to suggest a horizontally moving film title. [Fonts In Use](https://fontsinuse.com/uses/6396/der-film-exhibition-poster-and-catalog).

The eMuseum holds many preparatory photograms, drafts, and a construction drawing for the poster, for example [object 167053](https://www.emuseum.ch/objects/167053), donated by Shizuko Yoshikawa from the Müller-Brockmann archive.
observed: A near-black field fills the sheet. The title sits low, in the lower third, and runs off the left edge.
“der” is in warm gray and “Film” is in off-white; the F of Film overlaps the r of der, so the two words interlock.
All small text is red, in two blocks: the museum and “Ausstellung” at top, dates and opening hours at bottom.
Both red blocks start on the same vertical line, aligned with the left edge of the F.
The typeface is a grotesque in lowercase for the title and upper- and lowercase for the text; nothing is centered.
The upper two thirds of the sheet is empty except for the two red lines.
interpretation: The poster shows how the style gets motion without illustration: overlap and cropping of one word do the work of an image.
The single left axis shared by the red text and the capital F is a visible grid decision in a layout that otherwise looks free.
borrow: Hang all secondary text from one vertical axis and let the display word break it.
Use an empty field as the main surface. One very large word plus a few small lines can be a complete composition.
Overlap two weights or tints of the same word to suggest sequence or motion.

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons marks its copy PD-textlogo; this catalogue does not rely on that claim. Poster in copyright; no image is stored. Rights remain with the designer’s estate and the holding institutions. MoMA, the Museum für Gestaltung Zürich, and the Library of Congress (rights status not evaluated) hold copies.

references.title: Earth and City 10 (Expression of Ideas)
references.lede: A Korean stock composite of 2007: a glowing wireframe globe, an airliner, and a clean skyline over blue water and green banks.
references.summary: Glass globe, sky, water, and skyline in one stock image. Asadal, 2007.

evidence.note: Inspected the 1120 × 581 file [File:Earth and City 10 (Expression of ideas).jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Earth_and_City_10_(Expression_of_ideas).jpg) and stored it. Checked the license and date on the Gongu Madang record.

styles.note: A period stock image with the style’s central idea, technology in harmony with nature; Wikipedia uses it to illustrate that theme.

context: Gongu Madang (Korea Copyright Commission) records the work “지구와 도시 10(발상의 표현)” by 아사달 (Asadal), created 2007-10-29, a Photoshop composite, offered under CC BY. [Gongu record](https://gongu.copyright.or.kr/gongu/wrt/wrt/view.do?wrtSn=9046218&menuNo=200018).

The Wikipedia Frutiger Aero article uses this image for the claim that the style “often depicts the natural in tandem with digital elements.” [Wikipedia: Frutiger Aero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frutiger_Aero).

CARI links Asadal’s design mall to the style and published an interview with its CEO, Chang N. Suh (Yunseon Yang and Sofi Xian, June 2026). It reports that Asadal donated image assets to the Korea Copyright Commission for free use under CC BY. [The Future Is Aesthetic](https://sofixian.substack.com/p/frutiger-aero-and-the-story-of-asadal).
observed: A deep-blue sky fades to pale cyan at the horizon, with small white clouds.
A translucent, glowing globe at upper right is wrapped in white orbit lines and has a star-shaped lens flare at its edge.
An airliner at upper left trails a thin white line toward the globe.
Glass towers rise from green banks beside still blue water; a red arch bridge sits at the right edge.
Faint translucent hexagons float in the middle of the sky.
interpretation: This is the style as commercial stock: the “globe plus skyline plus nature” image that filled corporate web headers. Its mood is frictionless progress — clean air travel, clean water, clean city.
borrow: For a hero image, stack three layers: a blue sky gradient, a glowing translucent object (globe, orb, or bubble), and a green or water horizon.
Use one lens flare or star highlight as a focal accent, not many.

images.alt: Blue sky over a lake and green banks with a skyline of glass towers and a red bridge; a glowing translucent globe with orbit lines at upper right and an airliner at upper left.
images.caption: “Earth and City 10 (Expression of Ideas)” by Asadal, 2007. CC BY 4.0 via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Earth_and_City_10_(Expression_of_ideas).jpg), from [Gongu Madang](https://gongu.copyright.or.kr/gongu/wrt/wrt/view.do?wrtSn=9046218&menuNo=200018).

rights.statement: By Asadal. Offered under CC BY by the Korea Copyright Commission (Gongu Madang); Wikimedia Commons records CC BY 4.0.

references.title: Envato, “Trend Deep Dive: Neo-brutalism”
references.lede: A stock-marketplace trend brief that carries the name into print templates and social graphics.
references.summary: Envato’s 2023 brief for asset authors, covering UI, social media, and printed posters and flyers.

evidence.note: Article text read on 2026-09-25. Published 9 November 2023 per the page metadata.

styles.note: It uses the name “Neo-brutalism (AKA Neubrutalism)” and lists hard shadows, outlines, bold color, and no gradients as the style’s traits.

context: Key traits listed: “Bold modern typography”, “Bold and vibrant colors often with high contrast”, “Lack of gradients”, and “Hard shadows, dark contrasts and outlines”. It advises that shadows “should be black and should have 100% opacity”.

It applies the name beyond screens: templates “can be adapted to various mediums such as printed posters, flyers and designer portfolios”, and an Envato graphics reviewer encourages authors “to explore Neo-brutalism for print templates”.
Like Malewicz, it cites Figma and Gumroad as site examples.
interpretation: Evidence that by late 2023 the name was a commercial template category that spans print and social media, not only web UI.

rights.statement: © Envato. Link and quotation only.

references.title: Experimental Jetset website
references.lede: The Amsterdam studio’s online archive: a directory listing of every project, set in one size of Helvetica on a six-column grid.
references.summary: Six columns of project titles and dates in one size of black Helvetica on white, with finished projects struck through.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 25 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: A clear example of the grid and the type: every line sits in one of six columns, in black Helvetica, flush left. It has no scale contrast at all, so it fails the `type.sizeRange` metric (see the style page).

observed: A plain text header reads “Experimental Jetset” at the top left and “Search” at the top right.
A short vertical menu lists Archive (in bold), Preview, News, About, and Contact.
A thin black rule spans the page under the menu and a Categories drop-down.
Below the rule, six equal columns list project titles, each with a month and year aligned to the right of the column.
Many titles are struck through. All text is black on white and appears to be the same size.
interpretation: The measurement finds only Helvetica, only black and white, square corners, and no centered text. Every text run is 13.2 px, so the size range is 1.
The grid carries the whole page: the directory reads as a table because the columns are strict, not because of rules or boxes.
borrow: Let a long list become the layout: equal columns, one type size, and dates aligned to a fixed column edge.

images.alt: Experimental Jetset archive page: a small menu at the top left, a thin rule, and six dense columns of project titles with dates, all in small black Helvetica on white, many titles struck through.
images.caption: First viewport of [jetset.nl](https://www.jetset.nl/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to Experimental Jetset. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Figma marketing website, c. 2022
references.lede: Figma’s early-2020s marketing pages, named with Gumroad as a source of the style.
references.summary: Figma’s landing pages as described by Malewicz in March 2022.

evidence.note: Wayback Machine capture of figma.com from 28 February 2022, captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) and inspected on 25 September 2026.

styles.note: Malewicz (2022) names Figma and Gumroad as the “two main innovators” of neubrutalism, and NN/g repeats Figma as an example.

context: [Michał Malewicz, “Neubrutalism is taking over the web” (Hype4 Academy, first published 28 March 2022)](https://hype4.academy/articles/design/neubrutalism-is-taking-over-web) analyzes Figma landing-page sections: cards “purposefully inconsistent”, shapes like “template shapes from PowerPoint”, hard figure-to-background contrast, and thick, slightly quirky fonts.

[NN/g, “Neobrutalism: Definition and Best Practices” (Hayat Sheikh, 11 April 2025)](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/neobrutalism/) names “Figma's brand refresh” as an example, linking to [Figma’s October 2019 brand post](https://www.figma.com/blog/bringing-new-life-to-figmas-brand/) by Tori Hinn. That post predates the name and does not use it.
interpretation: The capture does not show the outline-and-hard-shadow grammar. It fails the fingerprint on outline width, radius, and shadows. Figma’s influence on the style, as Malewicz describes it, is in its playful stickers, bright accents, and hand-made marks, not in its layout components. The placement stays, but as an influence.
next: Check other Figma pages from 2021–2022, such as the Config and community pages, for stronger examples.

rights.statement: Figma’s design and content belong to Figma. Captured from the Internet Archive for commentary.

observed: White page with a centered black headline, “Nothing great is designed alone.”, in a large sans-serif. The word “designed” is violet inside a thin selection box with a cursor label.
Buttons are black with white text and rounded corners. No component has a thick outline or a hard shadow.
Below the hero, a mock Figma editor shows the product interface with small colorful stickers and a hand-drawn yellow stroke.

images.alt: Archived Figma home page: a white page with the headline “Nothing great is designed alone.” where “designed” is violet in a selection box, a black Try Figma for free button, and a mock editor interface with colorful stickers below.
images.caption: First viewport of the [February 2022 archived copy of figma.com](https://web.archive.org/web/20220228235551/https://www.figma.com/).

references.title: First chair
references.lede: Michele De Lucchi’s chair for Memphis: a metal hoop that carries a blue disc and two black balls.
references.summary: De Lucchi’s 1983 chair: tubular hoop, round seat, blue disc back, ball armrests.

source.label: National Gallery of Victoria: First, chair (D75-1985)

creator.name: Michele De Lucchi (designer); Memphis, Milan (manufacturer and retailer)

evidence.note: Downloaded the museum’s published image (694 × 859 px) from [the National Gallery of Victoria](https://www.ngv.vic.gov.au/explore/collection/work/20878/) to a private scratchpad and inspected it with the Read tool on 2026-09-25. No image is stored in the catalogue. The Met record was also read; it has no online image.

styles.note: Made and sold by Memphis; the Met calls it characteristic of the collective’s designs.

context: The NGV lists De Lucchi as designer and Memphis, Milan, as manufacturer and retailer; lacquered metal and wood, 90.3 × 66.2 × 46.2 cm, purchased in 1985. [NGV record](https://www.ngv.vic.gov.au/explore/collection/work/20878/).

The Met describes a black wooden seat disc on four tubular legs, with a tilted tubular hoop that carries a turquoise disc backrest and two black ball armrests. It calls the chair characteristic of the Memphis collective that De Lucchi co-founded with Sottsass. [Met record](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/753976), accession 2021.54.10.
observed: A gray tubular ring rises from the front legs and tilts back behind the seat.
A flat blue disc is fixed at the top of the ring as the backrest.
Two glossy black spheres sit on the ring at the sides as armrests.
The round seat is black, on four thin straight gray legs.
interpretation: The chair is drawn with lines and dots: a circle, a disc, and two balls. It shows that Memphis could be sparse. Here the play comes from geometry and a few colors, not from pattern.
borrow: Compose with a thin circular line and a few solid dots placed on it.
Let one saturated disc of color act as the focal point against black and gray.

rights.statement: The NGV allows its image to be downloaded for publications and non-commercial use and states that it believes the work to be in the public domain. The design is by a living designer and dates from 1983, so the catalogue treats it as in copyright and stores no image.

references.title: Fractal design system documentation
references.lede: The Storybook documentation of Snowball’s Fractal design system.
references.summary: Documentation site whose cover shows outlined, hard-shadowed swatch cards; the page chrome itself is plainer.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 25 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: The system is neo-brutalist, but the documentation page mostly is not. It fails the fingerprint on outline share and width.

observed: A black sidebar lists components. A flat pink top bar spans the content area.
The cover image shows swatch cards with black outlines and hard shadows in mint, violet, yellow, cyan, and pink.
The documentation text sits on an off-white page with a heavy sans-serif title and plain body text.
interpretation: Measurement separates the system from its documentation shell: the style lives in the components and the cover art, not in the Storybook frame. This is a useful case for the rule that a reference must show the style, not only describe it.

images.alt: Fractal Storybook page: a black sidebar of component names, a pink top bar, the title Fractal, and a cover image of colored swatch cards with black outlines and hard shadows.
images.caption: First viewport of [fractal.snowball.xyz](https://fractal.snowball.xyz/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to Snowball. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Fractal, Snowball’s design system
references.lede: A company design system that writes “brutal shadows” into its color documentation.
references.summary: Open-source fintech design system with black strokes, hard shadows, and pastel tones.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected `packages/fractal/public/images/cover_fractal.png` (3200 × 1800) from the repository. Licence read through the GitHub API. The Storybook site was not captured.

styles.note: The palette documentation names black as the color for “Strokes & Brutal shadows”, and swatch cards use black outlines and hard shadows.

context: The README describes “the open-source mono-repository for the design reference, components libraries and documentations of Fractal, Snowball’s design system”. Repository created 19 June 2023; MIT License, copyright 2023 Snowball. Documentation: [fractal.snowball.xyz](https://fractal.snowball.xyz/).
Listed under “Complete Design System” in the CC0 [Awesome Neobrutalism](https://github.com/ComradeAERGO/Awesome-Neobrutalism) list.
observed: Color swatch cards with black outlines and solid black shadows offset down and right.
Flat pastel and bright tones: mint, violet, yellow, cyan, and a primary pink #FF8ACD, with pure black #000000 as the secondary color.
The secondary color’s usage note lists “Strokes & Brutal shadows styles”.
Large heavy sans-serif headings on an off-white page.
interpretation: A production design system, not a demo kit. It shows the style formalized as tokens: one black for all strokes and shadows, and a tonal scale for each bright.
borrow: Reserve one color token for all outlines and hard shadows. Give each bright hue a few lighter tones for large backgrounds.
next: Capture the Storybook and snowball.xyz to measure outline width and shadow offset.

rights.statement: The repository is MIT-licensed, but the cover image includes the Snowball wordmark and a third-party emoji glyph, so it is not stored.

references.title: Frutiger typeface
references.lede: Adrian Frutiger’s humanist sans-serif for airport signs, and the other half of the style’s name.
references.summary: Open, legible humanist sans-serif. Adrian Frutiger, released 1976.
references.made: 1976 (public release by Stempel with Linotype; developed from the Roissy signage type of 1970/71)

evidence.note: Inspected the public-domain specimen [File:FrutigerSpec-1.svg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FrutigerSpec-1.svg), rendered by Wikimedia at 960 px wide, and stored it.

styles.note: The style is named partly after this typeface; its open humanist forms match the friendly type of the period, though the typeface itself was not the Aero interface font.

context: Frutiger is a humanist sans-serif by Adrian Frutiger. It is the text version of Roissy, commissioned in 1970/71 for the signs of Charles de Gaulle Airport, and was released publicly in 1976 by Stempel with Linotype. [Wikipedia: Frutiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frutiger_(typeface)).

CARI says the name joins Vista’s “Aero” guideline with Frutiger’s typeface, “which originally inspired Vista’s default font (Segoe UI).” [CARI: Frutiger Aero](https://cari.institute/aesthetics/frutiger-aero).

Avcı notes that Frutiger “was not used in the Aero, TouchWiz, or MacOS X interfaces associated with the movement,” so the name can mislead. [Avcı 2024, “Physical reflections of digital aesthetics”](https://doi.org/10.17932/IAU.EJNM.25480200.2024/ejnm_v8i3003), pp. 463–464. See [Segoe UI](ref:segoe-ui-typeface).
observed: Letters are open and round with wide apertures: the a, e, and c curl in only slightly.
The a is double-storey; the g is single-storey; the i has a square dot.
The large lowercase x-height makes the specimen’s lowercase nearly as tall as the capitals.
The specimen shows the airport phrase “Accès aux avions” in gray.
interpretation: The link to the style is typological, not literal: the era’s interfaces used humanist sans-serifs with the same openness and warmth, and Frutiger stands for that family in the name.
borrow: Pair glossy surfaces with an open humanist sans-serif, not a geometric or grotesque one. The warmth of the letters carries the “friendly technology” tone.

images.alt: Type specimen of Frutiger: the name in bold, “Aa Ee Rr” in regular and bold, a large white lowercase a, “Accès aux avions” in gray, and the lowercase alphabet and figures on a yellow band.
images.caption: Frutiger specimen by GearedBull, 2006, released into the public domain. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FrutigerSpec-1.svg), rendered from SVG to PNG by Wikimedia.

rights.statement: Specimen released into the public domain by its author (PD-user, GearedBull) on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FrutigerSpec-1.svg). Letterform designs are not copyrightable in the United States; the Frutiger name and font software belong to their owners.

references.title: Gabon textile samples
references.lede: Nathalie Du Pasquier’s screen-printed cotton Gabon: jagged shapes, checkered borders, and six colorways.
references.summary: Du Pasquier’s 1982 printed cotton: zigzag blocks and checkered bands in six colorways.

creator.name: Nathalie Du Pasquier (designer); produced by Rainbow, Milan

evidence.note: Downloaded the museum’s published image (843 px wide) from [the Art Institute of Chicago IIIF server](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/72939) to a private scratchpad and inspected it with the Read tool on 2026-09-25. No image is stored in the catalogue. The Met’s record of the same design was read; it has no online image.

styles.note: Du Pasquier was a Memphis member and a principal pattern designer for the group; this print shows the style’s surface language.

context: The Art Institute lists six samples of Gabon, designed by Nathalie Du Pasquier and produced by Rainbow, Milan, 1982; cotton twill, screen printed. The museum also holds her Zaire, Uganda, Kenya, Congo, Cameroon, and Zambia prints from the same year. [AIC record](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/72939).
The Met holds a full length of “Gabon” textile, 1982, cotton, 139.7 × 403.9 cm. [Met record](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/484547).
A 1983 Memphis leaflet by Christoph Radl labels “Gabon – 1982” among the group’s patterns. See [Memphis Milano leaflet](ref:radl-memphis-milano-leaflet-1983).
observed: Large jagged polygons in red, blue, green, purple, and white overlap one another.
Thick black outlines run around the shapes, broken by small checkered segments in white, blue, and pink.
Zigzag and stepped edges appear throughout; no curve is visible in the main swatch.
Five narrower strips show the same drawing in other colorways, including orange-red, teal-brown, and blue-black.
The samples hang from a black header card printed “RAINBOW”.
interpretation: The print is dense and uses clashing colors, and its checkered outline recurs in Memphis graphics and laminates. The colorway strips show that the drawing, not a single palette, carries the identity.
borrow: Outline flat shapes with a thick band that is itself patterned, such as a checkerboard.
Design one pattern and test it in several full-saturation colorways.

rights.statement: AIC marks the object as not public domain. No image is stored.

references.title: Giselle poster, Basler Freilichtspiele
references.lede: Armin Hofmann sets a vertical word against a blurred dancer: fixed geometry beside motion.
references.summary: Armin Hofmann, 1959. A rotated sans-serif title beside a black-and-white photograph of a spinning dancer.

source.label: eMuseum, Museum für Gestaltung Zürich: poster 39-0424

evidence.note: Downloaded SFMOMA’s web image of object 2014.669 (602 × 850 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. Catalogue data read on the eMuseum and SFMOMA records. The image is not stored.

styles.note: A key Basel-school poster: sans-serif type, a black-and-white photograph instead of illustration, and a strong asymmetric axis.

context: Poster for *Giselle* at the Basler Freilichtspiele, 1959. Design Armin Hofmann, photography Paul Merkle, printed by Wassermann AG, Basel. Offset, 127 × 90 cm, object 39-0424. [eMuseum, Museum für Gestaltung Zürich](https://www.emuseum.ch/objects/56272).

SFMOMA lists it as a lithograph, 128.0 × 90.4 cm, accession 2014.669, gift of Aaron Marcus, © Armin Hofmann. [SFMOMA](https://www.sfmoma.org/artwork/2014.669/). Cooper Hewitt also holds a copy (1997-19-142). [Smithsonian](https://www.si.edu/object/chndm_1997-19-142).

Wikipedia calls Hofmann one of the most influential figures of Swiss design and says his visiting professorship at Yale, from 1960 into the 1980s, introduced the Swiss style to the United States. [Wikipedia: Armin Hofmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armin_Hofmann).
observed: “Giselle” runs vertically up the left side in large off-white lowercase sans-serif, reading bottom to top.
The dot of the i is a separate white disc set away from the stem, near the middle of the sheet.
A blurred black-and-white photograph of a dancer in a tutu fills the right side; the motion blur makes the skirt a soft white streak.
Small flush-left text at top left gives festival, dates, and place in five short lines.
The palette is black, white, and grays; there is no added color.
interpretation: The poster pairs the two image types the style trusted: letterforms treated as geometry and a photograph treated as evidence. The contrast between hard type and soft blur is the message.
borrow: Rotate a single display word to form a vertical column that acts as the grid’s spine.
Let one photograph carry all the emotion and keep the type neutral.
Treat a detail of a letter, such as the i-dot, as an independent shape in the composition.

rights.statement: Poster in copyright; no image is stored. Rights remain with the designer’s estate and the holding institutions. SFMOMA states © Armin Hofmann.

references.title: Grid Systems in Graphic Design
references.lede: Josef Müller-Brockmann’s manual of the grid, with the grid itself drawn on its cover.
references.summary: Josef Müller-Brockmann, Niggli, 1981. The standard handbook of the typographic grid.

source.label: eMuseum, Museum für Gestaltung Zürich: A JMBR 181-1-6

evidence.note: Downloaded the cover scan [File:Raster-Systeme-Cover.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Raster-Systeme-Cover.jpg) (1200 × 1663 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. Interior pages were not seen. The image is not stored.

styles.note: A late summary of the style’s central method by one of its founders; the grid on the cover is the style’s structure made explicit.

context: *Rastersysteme für die visuelle Gestaltung / Grid systems in graphic design*, 1981; bilingual German and English, subtitled a handbook for graphic designers, typographers, and exhibition designers. The eMuseum holds the cover and several cover drafts from the Müller-Brockmann archive, donated by Shizuko Yoshikawa. [eMuseum object 167597](https://www.emuseum.ch/objects/167597).

Wikipedia’s bibliography lists it as published by Arthur Niggli, Niederteufen, 1981, ISBN 9783721201451. [Wikipedia: Josef Müller-Brockmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josef_M%C3%BCller-Brockmann).
Müller-Brockmann was a founding editor of [Neue Grafik](ref:neue-grafik-journal-1958-1965) and designed [Der Film](ref:der-film-poster-1960).
observed: The cover is a flat orange with a grid of thin white lines: four columns and several rows separated by narrow gutters.
Black grotesque type sits exactly on the grid. The two titles, “Grid systems” and “Raster systeme”, are the largest elements and start at the left margin.
Subtitles and the author’s name are small and flush left, starting either at the left margin or at the third column line.
The publisher’s name “Niggli” sits alone near the bottom, on the same column line as the author’s name.
Only three colors appear: orange, black, and white.
interpretation: Showing the grid lines on the cover makes the invisible structure of the style visible, and turns a method into an image.
borrow: Start text blocks on only two or three column lines, and repeat those lines throughout the layout.
Consider revealing the grid as thin lines when the subject is structure or documentation.
Use one saturated flat background color with black type and white rules.

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons marks its cover scan as public domain; this catalogue does not rely on that claim. The book remains in copyright; no image is stored.

references.title: Gumroad website and brand, 2021
references.lede: The creator-commerce platform’s tenth-anniversary redesign, the example most often cited for the style.
references.summary: Gumroad’s November 2021 brand and website, cited by Malewicz and NN/g as neo-brutalist.

evidence.note: Wayback Machine capture of gumroad.com from 15 January 2022, captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) and inspected on 25 September 2026, plus the founder’s announcement graphic. The live site was also inspected on that date and no longer shows the style.

styles.note: Malewicz (2022) calls Gumroad one of the “two main innovators” of neubrutalism, and NN/g (2025) uses it as an example.

context: On 26 November 2021 Sahil Lavingia wrote: “Gumroad is ten years old, and we're beginning the next 10 years worth of bets with a new brand (and website, fonts, colors, and more!)” ([announcement](https://sahil.gumroad.com/p/introducing-the-new-gumroad)). The linked essay “Betting on the new Gumroad” is archived from the same day.

[Michał Malewicz, “Neubrutalism is taking over the web” (Hype4 Academy, first published 28 March 2022)](https://hype4.academy/articles/design/neubrutalism-is-taking-over-web) names Figma and Gumroad as the style’s “two main innovators” and describes Gumroad’s mix of illustration, photography, fake 3D, and parallax.
[NN/g, “Neobrutalism: Definition and Best Practices” (Hayat Sheikh, 11 April 2025)](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/neobrutalism/) cites Gumroad as an example of neobrutalism in practice.
Gumroad’s code was released on GitHub under the MIT License in 2025 ([antiwork/gumroad](https://github.com/antiwork/gumroad)). That licence does not clearly cover the brand artwork.
observed: Archived home page (January 2022): the gumroad wordmark runs across the full width in huge black letters.
Navigation links sit in a row divided by thin black rules. Start Selling is a black block.
The hero splits into a flat pink panel and a flat yellow panel. The yellow panel holds a photo of a woman cut out with a thick black outline, plus outlined sticker illustrations.
Type is a single grotesque family (Mabry Pro), black on white or on color. The Start Selling button is a square black rectangle.
No component showed a shadow at rest in the measurement.
In the announcement graphic: pink “G” discs with black outlines and solid black extrusions on a flat yellow blob.
interpretation: The archived home page shows the flat-bright, black-outline, square-corner side of the style but not hard offset shadows at rest. Either the shadows appear only in hover states and deeper pages, or hard shadows are less central to the style than the fingerprint assumes. This record is calibration evidence for the fingerprint.
borrow: Let the brand illustration use the same outline weight and hard depth as the interface components.
next: Check hover states and product pages in the same capture for hard offset shadows.
Capture a December 2021 copy for comparison with the January 2022 one.

rights.statement: Gumroad’s design and content belong to Gumroad. Captured from the Internet Archive for commentary.

references.notice: The live gumroad.com no longer uses this design. On 25 September 2026 it had a black background, rounded cards (median radius 25 px), 1 px borders, and no shadows. This record describes the 2021–2022 design through an archived copy.

images.alt: Archived Gumroad home page: the gumroad wordmark in huge black letters across the top, a navigation row divided by thin black rules, a pink hero panel with the headline “Go from zero to $1” and a black Start Selling button, and a yellow panel with a photo of a woman outlined in black with sticker illustrations.
images.caption: Viewport capture of the [January 2022 Wayback copy of gumroad.com](https://web.archive.org/web/20220115112257/https://gumroad.com/).

references.title: Gunta Stölzl, design for the wall hanging “Fünf Chöre”
references.lede: A Jacquard wall-hanging design on squared paper: bands of stripes, triangles, and half-circles in a symmetrical grid.
references.summary: Stripes, triangles, and small circles in bands on a grid. Gunta Stölzl, Bauhaus Dessau weaving workshop, 1928.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected, in the scratchpad only, the Bauhaus-Archiv image of the design on the Bauhaus Kooperation page (710 × 917 px).

styles.note: Bauhaus weaving: elementary triangles, circles, and bars placed on a strict grid for machine production.

context: From 1926 Anni Albers and Gunta Stölzl worked with the Jacquard technique, in which punched cards lift single warp threads. Bauhaus Kooperation links this to the Dessau aim of production at scale. [Bauhaus Kooperation](https://bauhauskooperation.de/wissen/das-bauhaus/werke/weberei/fuenf-choere/).

Stölzl planned the hanging for a larger edition. One example is in the Museum für Kunst und Kulturgeschichte, Lübeck; a second is lost. Jeroen Vinken (2013) questions whether the title is correct. [Bauhaus Kooperation](https://bauhauskooperation.de/wissen/das-bauhaus/werke/weberei/fuenf-choere/).
observed: The design is painted on squared paper, with thread counts in pencil down the right side.
Horizontal bands repeat rows of triangles, half-circles, small dots, checks, and vertical stripes.
The layout is mirror-symmetrical, with a wider central column and two side columns.
Colors are muted: ochre, pink, green, and gray, with accents of red, blue, and black.
Color test patches sit in the lower right margin.
interpretation: The design uses the Bauhaus shape vocabulary but not its primary palette. It is a good case of the rubric’s limit: elementary shapes and a grid are present, while the colors are softer than the style’s “primary triad” guidance.
The grid and repeat show the Dessau move toward designs for production.
borrow: Build a pattern from bands, each band using one elementary shape repeated at a fixed interval.
Use strict symmetry across a few columns to calm a dense pattern.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Bauhaus Kooperation credits its image “Bauhaus-Archiv Berlin / © VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn.” Stölzl died in 1983.

references.title: Helvetica typeface
references.lede: Neue Haas Grotesk, renamed Helvetica: a denser, smoother Akzidenz for the Swiss market that became the style’s best-known letter.
references.summary: Max Miedinger and Eduard Hoffmann, Haas Type Foundry, 1956–1957; renamed Helvetica for Linotype.

creator.name: Max Miedinger, under the direction of Eduard Hoffmann (Haas Type Foundry)

references.made: 1956–1957 (as Neue Haas Grotesk); adapted for Linotype and renamed Helvetica in 1959, per Wikipedia

evidence.note: Inspected and stored the public-domain raster specimen [File:HelveticaSpecimenCH.png](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:HelveticaSpecimenCH.png). It shows a digital Helvetica, not the 1957 metal type.

styles.note: Wikipedia calls it a hallmark of the International Typographic Style, and the style file lists it among the core grotesques.

context: Helvetica was designed in 1956–1957 by Max Miedinger under the direction of Eduard Hoffmann of the Haas Type Foundry in Münchenstein, near Basel, as Neue Haas Grotesk. It is based chiefly on [Akzidenz-Grotesk](ref:akzidenz-grotesk-typeface), and Haas developed it to compete with that face in Switzerland. [Wikipedia: Helvetica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helvetica).

It was adapted for Linotype machines and renamed Helvetica, Latin for Swiss, at Hoffmann’s suggestion. Wikipedia dates the adaptation and renaming to 1959. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helvetica).

Wikipedia describes a high x-height, strokes that end on horizontals or verticals, and tight spacing. It calls the face a hallmark of the International Typographic Style. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helvetica).

Unimark International used Helvetica widely but not exclusively. [Wikipedia: Unimark International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unimark_International). See [NYCTA Graphics Standards Manual](ref:nycta-graphics-standards-manual-1970).
observed: Terminals of a, c, e, and s end horizontally, so the counters look closed and the letters look compact.
The lowercase is tall relative to the capitals; the large white a nearly fills the upper right of the specimen.
Letters sit close together in the word “Kunstgewerbeschule”, which reads as one dense band.
The specimen uses gray, black, white, and one red, laid out flush left.
interpretation: Helvetica is the style’s letter made smooth and even. Compared with Akzidenz-Grotesk, it trades small irregularities for uniform texture, which helped it spread from posters into corporate identity and signage.
borrow: Set tight but not touching. Horizontal terminals give a solid, closed texture that holds up at large display sizes.
Use the tall x-height for small text in signage and captions.

images.alt: Type specimen of Helvetica: the name in light gray, “Aa Ee Rr” in roman and italic, a large white bold lowercase a, the word “Kunstgewerbeschule” in red, and the lowercase alphabet and figures on a red band.
images.caption: Helvetica specimen by Dioxaz after a sample by GearedBull, 2006, released into the public domain. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:HelveticaSpecimenCH.png).

rights.statement: Released into the public domain by its author (PD-user, Dioxaz) on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:HelveticaSpecimenCH.png). Letterform designs are not copyrightable in the United States. Helvetica is a trademark; the name and font software belong to their owners.

references.title: Herbert Bayer, Research in Development of Universal Type
references.lede: Bayer’s single-case alphabet drawn from arcs and straight strokes, the reference point for Bauhaus lowercase typography.
references.summary: A lowercase-only geometric alphabet built from circles and bars. Herbert Bayer, drawing dated 1927 by Harvard; the alphabet is usually dated 1925.

source.label: Harvard Art Museums: Research in Development of Universal Type (BR48.94)

evidence.note: Based on the Harvard Art Museums record and the Bauhaus Kooperation workshop page. The museum image did not download (HTTP 403), so no image of the drawing was inspected. A digital “universal” specimen on Commons was not used because it is a modern revival, not Bayer’s drawing.

styles.note: The style summary names Bayer’s universal alphabet as the source of Bauhaus lowercase, geometric sans-serif type.

references.notice: No image is stored. The drawing is still in copyright (© Artists Rights Society / VG Bild-Kunst).
context: Harvard dates the drawing 1927 and describes it as black ink and gouache on cream wove paper, 37.5 × 60.4 cm. Bayer gave it to the Busch-Reisinger Museum in 1948. [Harvard BR48.94](https://harvardartmuseums.org/collections/object/225330).

Graphite notes in Bayer’s hand read “abbildung 1. alfabet. g und k ist noch als unfertig zu betrachten” (figure 1, alphabet; g and k are to be considered unfinished) and “beispiel eines zeichnens in grösserem massta[b] präcise optische wirkung.” [Harvard BR48.94](https://harvardartmuseums.org/collections/object/225330).

Bauhaus Kooperation says Bayer based his type design on the simplest geometric elements, with the goal of standardizing communication and a uniform typographic identity for the Bauhaus; the workshop’s type reform was most visible in the use of lowercase only. [Bauhaus Kooperation: Druck und Reklame](https://bauhauskooperation.de/wissen/das-bauhaus/lehre/werkstaetten/druck-und-reklame).

Bayer led the Dessau printing and advertising workshop from 1925 to 1928. [Bauhaus Kooperation: Herbert Bayer](https://bauhauskooperation.de/wissen/das-bauhaus/koepfe/biografien/biografie-detail/person-59).
interpretation: The universal alphabet is more a program than a working typeface: one case, a few construction elements, and no historical ornament. It explains why lowercase headings read as “Bauhaus”.
borrow: Set headings in lowercase only, in a geometric sans-serif with circular bowls.
Treat a type system as a small kit of arcs and straight strokes, and keep it consistent across all printed matter.
next: Inspect an image of BR48.94 (Harvard image service or the MoMA 2009 catalogue, cat. no. 258) and add observed traits.

rights.statement: Harvard Art Museums lists the copyright as © Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York / VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn. Bayer died in 1985.

references.title: Kandinsky’s postcard for the 1923 Bauhaus exhibition
references.lede: Card no. 3 of the exhibition series: Kandinsky’s circles, checkerboards, and crossing lines under plain sans-serif capitals.
references.summary: Blue ring, red arc, checkerboard, and diagonal lines. Wassily Kandinsky, printed postcard, 1923.

source.label: Philadelphia Museum of Art: Postcard No. 3 for the Bauhaus Exhibition

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the [Commons scan](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Postkarte_Bauhaus_Wassily_Kandinsky_Postkarte_f%C3%BCr_die_Bauhaus-Ausstellung.jpg) (539 × 805 px). Commons gives a Villa Grisebach auction as its source.

styles.note: Elementary shapes used as composition elements, primary accents, and sans-serif lettering, by a Bauhaus master for the school’s first exhibition.

context: The Philadelphia Museum of Art catalogues the card as “Postcard No. 3 for the Bauhaus Exhibition, Weimar, July–September 1923.” Its text says the exhibition answered a demand from the Thuringian State Assembly for a progress report, and that it put architecture at the center with an emphasis on joining art and technology. [PMA 255859](https://www.philamuseum.org/objects/255859).

The card belongs to a series of 20 postcards for the exhibition, by Feininger, Kandinsky, Klee, Moholy-Nagy, Schlemmer, Bayer, and others. [Bauhaus-Karten](https://www.bauhaus-postkarten.de/karten/nr.3-wassily-kandinsky/). MoMA also holds a copy. [MoMA 133652](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/133652).
observed: A blue disc in a black ring floats at upper right; a small black dot and a black square sit nearby.
A large maroon disc at lower left is cut by a red arc and a white wedge.
Long thin black lines cross the card on several diagonals; two ladder-like bands carry small red, blue, and white blocks.
A black-and-white checkerboard square sits at left.
The lettering is thin, even-weight sans-serif capitals: “BAU- HAUS- AUSSTELLUNG WEIMAR” and “JULI – SEPTEMBER 1923”.
The ground is plain cream paper.
interpretation: The card links Kandinsky’s teaching on point, line, and plane to the exhibition’s public face. The shapes are active and diagonal, but the lettering stays quiet and upright.
Compared with Schmidt’s poster, this is the freer, painterly side of Bauhaus geometry.
borrow: Set small, precise areas of primary color against many thin black lines.
Keep the text in one plain sans-serif weight so that the composition carries the energy.

images.alt: Cream postcard with a blue disc in a black ring, a maroon disc cut by a red arc, a checkerboard square, and many thin crossing diagonal lines. Thin sans-serif capitals read Bauhaus-Ausstellung Weimar, Juli–September 1923.
images.caption: Wassily Kandinsky, postcard no. 3 for the 1923 Bauhaus exhibition. Scan on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Postkarte_Bauhaus_Wassily_Kandinsky_Postkarte_f%C3%BCr_die_Bauhaus-Ausstellung.jpg), public domain.

rights.statement: Marked public domain on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Postkarte_Bauhaus_Wassily_Kandinsky_Postkarte_f%C3%BCr_die_Bauhaus-Ausstellung.jpg). Kandinsky died in 1944, and the card was published in 1923. The scan is a faithful reproduction of a two-dimensional work.

references.title: Karl Gerstner’s grid for Capital
references.lede: A 58-unit layout grid that divides evenly into two, three, four, five, or six columns.
references.summary: Karl Gerstner’s “mobile” grid for the magazine Capital, c. 1962, published in Designing Programmes (1964).

source.label: Manuel Schmalstieg: Karl Gerstner’s layout grid

references.made: c. 1962 (grid); 1964 (published in Programme entwerfen / Designing Programmes)

evidence.note: Relies on Schmalstieg’s note and the Commons description. The stored image is a 2018 visualization by Manuel Schmalstieg, based on the reproduction in *Designing Programmes*. It is not the original drawing, and no page of *Capital* was seen.

styles.note: The best-known example of the style’s modular grid used as a flexible program, not a fixed template.

context: Karl Gerstner designed a layout grid for the German business magazine *Capital* in 1962–1963 and presented it in his book *Designing Programmes*. The grid is based on 58 modules. [Schmalstieg](https://ms-studio.net/notes/karl-gerstners-layout-grid/); [Commons file description](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Karl_Gerstner_Capital_layout_grid.png).

The arithmetic: with 2-unit gutters, 58 = 2 × 28 + 2 = 3 × 18 + 2 × 2 = 4 × 13 + 3 × 2 = 5 × 10 + 4 × 2 = 6 × 8 + 5 × 2. So one grid carries two to six columns without remainder. [Designing Programmes excerpt](https://medium.com/@digitalonetwo/designing-programmes-excerpt-62bc64e67b8b).

Gerstner, a Basel typographer, co-founded the agency Gerstner+Kutter in 1958 (GGK from 1962). *Programme entwerfen* was published by Arthur Niggli in 1964; MoMA showed an exhibition based on it in 1973. [Wikipedia: Karl Gerstner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Gerstner).
observed: The visualization shows a large square divided into four quadrants. Each quadrant is subdivided by overlapping, semi-transparent bands of modules in muted greens, pinks, and yellows.
Where bands of different column systems overlap, small squares of darker or different tint mark the shared module lines.
Several separate single squares in pale colors stand to the left of the main grid.
All shapes are rectangles with thin dark outlines; there are no curves and no type. The colors are the visualizer’s, not Gerstner’s.
interpretation: The grid is the style’s answer to variety: instead of many templates, one fine module that several column counts share. Designers can change layout from page to page and still keep every edge on the system.
borrow: For responsive web layouts, choose a column unit count that divides evenly into 2, 3, 4, and 6 (for example 12 or 24), or follow Gerstner’s approach and include gutters in the arithmetic.
Document a grid as a program: the rules for dividing it, not one fixed picture.

images.alt: Diagram of a square layout grid divided into four quadrants, each overlaid with translucent colored bands that mark two-, three-, four-, five-, and six-column divisions; several single pale squares stand to the left.
images.caption: Visualization of the 58-unit grid designed by Karl Gerstner for *Capital*, c. 1962, by Manuel Schmalstieg, 2018, based on the reproduction in *Designing Programmes*. CC BY-SA 4.0. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Karl_Gerstner_Capital_layout_grid.png).

rights.statement: Diagram © Manuel Schmalstieg, licensed [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/) on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Karl_Gerstner_Capital_layout_grid.png). It is a new drawing of a layout system (a set of divisions), not a reproduction of Gerstner’s printed pages. Stored as a reduced PNG.

references.title: KDE Plasma 4 desktop
references.lede: Free-software desktop of the late 2000s with glassy widgets, glowing bubbles on teal, and a wallpaper of wet grass.
references.summary: Translucent widgets, teal bubble wallpaper, dew on grass. KDE, 2008 onward.

evidence.note: Inspected the GPL-licensed screenshot [File:Plasma Workspaces.png](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Plasma_Workspaces.png) (1652 × 996, 2011) and stored a 1600 px copy.

styles.note: Wikipedia uses this screenshot as its lead example of the style: glass widgets, bubbles, water drops, and grass.

context: KDE Plasma 4 is the fourth generation of KDE’s workspaces (desktop, netbook, and tablet). KDE 4.0 was released in January 2008. From KDE 4.3 the default Air theme “predominates in transparency and white.” [Wikipedia: KDE Plasma 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KDE_Plasma_4).

The lead image of the Wikipedia Frutiger Aero article is this screenshot, captioned: many interfaces from the 2000s “exemplify the Frutiger Aero style.” [Wikipedia: Frutiger Aero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frutiger_Aero).
The screenshot comes from a KDE developer’s blog post of March 2011 ([notmart.org](http://notmart.org/blog/2011/03/towards_a_declarative_plasma_co/)).
observed: A teal-to-dark-cyan wallpaper holds glowing, translucent bubbles and rings.
An image-viewer window shows a photograph of green grass blades covered in water drops.
Widgets (weather, contacts, launchers) are semi-transparent dark panels with rounded corners, soft glows, and glossy icons.
A tablet-style shell uses a magenta-to-orange gradient with large white rounded-square buttons.
interpretation: This is the style outside Microsoft and Apple: an open-source desktop reaching for the same glass, water, and dew imagery. It shows the look was a period consensus, not one company’s brand.
borrow: Put small content panels on a dark translucent fill with a 1 px light edge and rounded corners.
Use soft out-of-focus bubbles or rings as background texture instead of noise or patterns.

images.caption: KDE Plasma Workspaces, 2011, by KDE. GPL. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Plasma_Workspaces.png).

references.title: Mac OS X Aqua interface
references.lede: Apple’s water-themed interface: gel buttons, droplet controls, and reflective surfaces that set up the gloss of the later style.
references.summary: Gel buttons, translucent droplets, and a reflective Dock. Apple, 2000 onward.
references.made: Introduced January 2000; first released July 2000 with iMovie 2 and in Mac OS X 10.0 in 2001

evidence.note: Inspected two non-free screenshots in scratchpad copies: [File:Macosxpb.png](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Macosxpb.png) (Mac OS X Public Beta, 365 × 273) and [File:Leopard Desktop.png](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leopard_Desktop.png) (Mac OS X Leopard, 800 × 500). Not stored.

styles.note: Aqua introduced the water-like, glossy, translucent controls that Frutiger Aero inherits; it is a precursor more than a full example.

context: Aqua “was themed to replicate water, with ‘droplet-like’ components and a heavy use of reflective effects and translucency.” It was introduced at Macworld in January 2000, first shipped with iMovie 2 in July 2000, and with Mac OS X 10.0 the following year. [Wikipedia: Aqua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqua_(user_interface)).
Before OS X Yosemite (2014), most Aqua controls had a “glass” or “gel” effect. Apple moved to flat design in 2013. [Wikipedia: Aqua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqua_(user_interface)).
CARI lists “Aqua” as an alternate name for Frutiger Aero. [CARI: Frutiger Aero](https://cari.institute/aesthetics/frutiger-aero).
observed: Public Beta (2000): windows have pinstriped gray bars, red, yellow, and green gel buttons, and translucent blue highlighted menu items.
Public Beta: the Dock at the bottom holds glossy, shaded icons on a translucent strip.
Leopard (2007): the desktop picture is a magenta and violet aurora with stars; the Dock is a reflective glass shelf with icons mirrored below.
Leopard: window chrome is gray and brushed rather than pinstriped; blue folder icons are soft and rounded.
interpretation: Aqua supplies the gloss, gel, and reflection. Frutiger Aero adds bright daylight nature imagery and humanist type to that surface. Leopard’s aurora picture shows the two converging by 2007.
borrow: Use a floor reflection under a row of icons to suggest a glass shelf.
Give small status buttons a gel look: saturated color, a white highlight, and a dark rim.

rights.statement: Apple software; copyrighted. No image is stored here.

references.title: Marcel Breuer, club chair B 3 (“Wassily”)
references.lede: The first tubular steel armchair for the home: a cubic frame of bent tubes with fabric straps for seat, back, and arms.
references.summary: Bent steel tube frame with taut dark fabric straps. Marcel Breuer, Bauhaus Dessau, 1925–26.
references.made: 1926 (second version, per Bauhaus Kooperation); first version 1925

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected, in the scratchpad only, the Stiftung Bauhaus Dessau photograph on the Bauhaus Kooperation page and a [side view by Sailko](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Marcel_breuer,_poltrona_B_3,_1925,_01.JPG) of the example in the Musée national d’art moderne, Paris.

styles.note: The style summary names tubular steel as a Bauhaus material; this chair made it a domestic furniture type.

context: Bauhaus Kooperation says Breuer, the junior master in charge of the Dessau furniture workshop, designed the chair in 1926 as a showpiece of new living; it was later called “Wassily” after Wassily Kandinsky, and it furnished the Dessau Bauhaus building. [Bauhaus Kooperation](https://bauhauskooperation.de/wissen/das-bauhaus/werke/tischlerei/clubsessel-b-3-2-version/).

The Commons photograph labels the Paris example “B 3, 1925.” [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Marcel_breuer,_poltrona_B_3,_1925,_01.JPG). MoMA dates its example 1927–1928. [MoMA 2851](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/2851).
observed: The frame is made of thin metal tubes with a worn, dull plating, bent into rectangles with rounded corners.
Seen from the side, the base, arms, and back form overlapping rectangles and one strong diagonal.
Dark fabric straps stretch between the tubes to form the seat, the back, and the arm rests.
Screws and joins in the frame are visible.
The chair is open: the floor and the wall show through it from every side.
interpretation: The chair turns the poster grammar of bars and one diagonal into a structure. Tubular steel and canvas are shown as they are.
borrow: Draw with thin continuous lines and rounded corners only where a material bends.
Let one diagonal cross an otherwise orthogonal frame.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Commons photograph is CC BY 3.0, but the chair design is still protected; Breuer died in 1981. Bauhaus Kooperation’s photograph is credited to Stiftung Bauhaus Dessau / Kelly Kellerhoff.

references.title: Marianne Brandt, tea infuser MT 49
references.lede: A small metal teapot composed of a hemisphere, a disc, a cylinder, and a half-circle handle on a cross-shaped foot.
references.summary: Hemisphere body, flat cylindrical lid, half-disc ebony handle, cross foot. Marianne Brandt, Bauhaus metal workshop, 1924.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected Lucia Moholy’s 1924 photograph of the infuser on the Bauhaus Kooperation page, in the scratchpad only. The Met record gives materials and dimensions.

styles.note: A key object of the Bauhaus metal workshop: elementary solids and a half-circle handle, with no ornament.

context: Bauhaus Kooperation says Brandt made the infuser in her first year of study, 1924, in the metal workshop under László Moholy-Nagy, and that the Bauhaus often criticized the use of costly materials such as silver and ebony. [Bauhaus Kooperation](https://bauhauskooperation.de/wissen/das-bauhaus/werke/metall/tee-extraktkaennchen-mt-49).
The Met holds an example: “Tea Infuser and Strainer,” ca. 1924, silver and ebony, 8.3 × 10.8 × 16.5 cm, accession 2000.63a–c. [The Met 491299](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/491299).
observed: The body is a polished metal hemisphere that reflects its surroundings.
A flat disc lid sits on a short cylinder; a small black cylindrical knob sits on top.
The handle is a flat black half-disc, fixed to the body with a rectangular bracket.
A short straight spout projects at left.
The body rests on a small crossed foot.
interpretation: The infuser shows the Bauhaus approach to form in three dimensions: each part is one elementary solid, and the parts meet without transitions. It is the object equivalent of circles and bars in a poster.
borrow: Build a component from separate elementary shapes and keep the joins visible.
Contrast one polished or bright material with one flat black part.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Bauhaus Kooperation credits its photograph “Bauhaus-Archiv Berlin / © VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn.” The Met marks its record as not public domain. Brandt died in 1983 or 1984 (sources differ).

references.title: Memphis logotype drawing
references.lede: Christoph Radl’s artwork for the Memphis wordmark: squared white capitals over a patterned underline.
references.summary: Radl’s 1982 drawing of the blocky MEMPHIS wordmark on black.

creator.name: Christoph Radl (designer); Sottsass Associati and Memphis (clients)

evidence.note: Downloaded the museum’s published image (640 × 466 px) from [the Stedelijk Museum](https://www.stedelijk.nl/en/collection/92798-christoph-radl-memphis) to a private scratchpad and inspected it with the Read tool on 2026-09-25. No image is stored in the catalogue. The museum’s file carries a “NO REPRO QUALITY” stamp.

styles.note: The group’s own wordmark, drawn by its graphic designer.

context: The Stedelijk classes this as a drawing by Christoph Radl, 1982, 34.7 × 47.5 cm, with Sottsass Associati and Memphis as clients. [Stedelijk record](https://www.stedelijk.nl/en/collection/92798-christoph-radl-memphis).

*Interni* says Radl began working with Ettore Sottsass in 1980, “designing the image of Memphis”, and later curated the 2022 Triennale exhibition “Memphis Again”. [Interni: Memphis Again](https://www.internimagazine.com/agenda/memphis-again/).
observed: White capitals “MEMPHIS” sit on a black rectangle mounted on a white board.
The letters are built from rectangles; the M has a notched, stepped middle, and some strokes end in angled cuts.
Under each letter group runs a short bar of fine black-and-white pattern, broken into segments.
Tape and registration marks around the board show that it is working artwork.
interpretation: The wordmark is heavy and simple, which lets it sit on top of the group’s busy patterns. The patterned underline brings the laminate language into the type.
borrow: Pair a heavy, squared display wordmark with a thin patterned rule under it.
Put the wordmark in white on a solid black band when it must work over pattern.
references.related: The same letterforms appear on the [Memphis swatch card](ref:memphis-printed-cotton-swatch-1985) and the [1983 leaflet](ref:radl-memphis-milano-leaflet-1983).

rights.statement: The Stedelijk links to a general copyright page; no open license is stated. No image is stored.

references.title: Memphis Milano leaflet
references.lede: Christoph Radl’s 1983 Memphis leaflet: a catalogue grid of lamps under a row of labelled pattern swatches.
references.summary: Radl’s 1983 Memphis leaflet: labelled laminate and textile patterns over a grid of lamps.

creator.name: Christoph Radl (designer); Sottsass Associati (client); Memphis (publisher); Occhipinti (printer)

evidence.note: Downloaded the museum’s published image (500 × 364 px) from [the Stedelijk Museum](https://www.stedelijk.nl/en/collection/92956-christoph-radl-memphis-milano) to a private scratchpad and inspected it with the Read tool on 2026-09-25. No image is stored in the catalogue. The object has four parts; the image shows one side of one part. The record classes it as graphic design and does not say “leaflet”; that word is the catalogue’s description from the image and the 34.2 × 98.5 cm size.

styles.note: Official Memphis printed matter by the group’s graphic designer, showing its patterns and products together.

context: The Stedelijk lists Christoph Radl as designer, Sottsass Associati as client, Memphis as publisher, and Occhipinti as printer; 1983; 34.2 × 98.5 cm; four parts. [Stedelijk record](https://www.stedelijk.nl/en/collection/92956-christoph-radl-memphis-milano).

*Interni* says Radl began working with Ettore Sottsass in 1980, “designing the image of Memphis”, and later curated the 2022 Triennale exhibition “Memphis Again”. [Interni: Memphis Again](https://www.internimagazine.com/agenda/memphis-again/).
observed: A top row of pattern swatches is labelled by designer, name, and year, for example Nathalie Du Pasquier “Gabon” 1982 and Ettore Sottsass “Rete” and “Schizzo”.
The swatches include black-and-white nets and squiggles and bright color prints in pink, blue, yellow, and red.
A black band carries the “MEMPHIS MILANO” wordmark in blocky white letters.
Below, a grid of numbered photographs on black shows lamps by Bedin, Thun, Sottsass, De Lucchi, and others, each captioned with name and year.
interpretation: The leaflet treats patterns as products: laminates and textiles get the same captioned cells as lamps. For a website, the grid shows a way to lay out a Memphis catalogue without losing order.
borrow: Put pattern swatches in a strict captioned grid so the pattern is loud but the layout stays calm.
Use black cells behind product photographs so saturated objects stand out.
references.related: Pattern shown here: [Gabon](ref:du-pasquier-gabon-textile-1982). Wordmark study: [Radl’s logotype drawing](ref:radl-memphis-logotype-drawing-1982).

rights.statement: The Stedelijk links to a general copyright page; no open license is stated. No image is stored.

references.title: Memphis printed cotton swatch card
references.lede: A sample card of Memphis printed cottons under a black header with the group’s blocky wordmark.
references.summary: 1985 Memphis swatch: tilted turquoise squares on red under a MEMPHIS header card.

creator.name: Memphis (designer, as recorded by the V&A)

evidence.note: Downloaded the museum’s published image (843 px wide) from [the V&A IIIF server](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O294419/) to a private scratchpad and inspected it with the Read tool on 2026-09-25. No image is stored in the catalogue. The V&A record gives no pattern title or individual designer.

styles.note: A Memphis trade sample that joins the group’s printed pattern with its graphic identity.

context: The V&A records a swatch of printed cottons, Italy, 1985, with Memphis as designer. [V&A record](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O294419/).
The record does not name the pattern or the designer of the header card.
observed: A black header strip carries “MEMPHIS” in white, squared capitals with cut and notched strokes.
The front swatch shows turquoise squares, tilted at different angles, on a red ground.
Behind it, pinked edges of other fabrics show yellow, orange, and black.
The swatches are fixed to a plain white card with the accession number written below.
interpretation: The letterforms on the header look like Christoph Radl’s 1982 Memphis logotype drawing ([record](ref:radl-memphis-logotype-drawing-1982)). This is a visual comparison; the V&A does not name the designer.
Tilted squares scattered on a strong ground is the simplest version of the Memphis “confetti” pattern.
borrow: Scatter one simple shape at random angles over a contrasting solid ground.
Pair a busy pattern with a black band that carries the brand in heavy white lettering.

rights.statement: The V&A image is credited © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. No image is stored.

references.title: Munich 1972 Olympic pictograms
references.lede: Otl Aicher’s sport pictograms: figures drawn only with circles and bars on a 45-degree and 90-degree grid.
references.summary: Otl Aicher and the Munich organizing committee’s visual design department, 1972.

creator.name: Otl Aicher and Abteilung XI für visuelle Gestaltung, Organisationskomitee der XX. Olympischen Spiele München

evidence.note: Downloaded two CC BY 1.0 photographs by Henning Schlottmann of the pictograms still on site in Munich ([swimming hall](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Olympic_games_1972_pictogramms_swimming_hall_0525.JPG), [Olympiazentrum station](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Olympic_games_1972_pictogramms_olympic_station_0877.JPG)) to a scratch folder and inspected them. Poster data read on eMuseum record 230065. No image is stored.

styles.note: Aicher applied the style’s grid and objectivity to a wayfinding system; the pictograms are geometry on a fixed angular grid, without illustration.

context: Otl Aicher co-founded and taught at the Ulm School of Design and led the design team of the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, overseeing its system of pictograms. [Wikipedia: Otl Aicher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otl_Aicher).

Wikipedia’s history-of-design article quotes Michael Bierut praising the pictograms for their elegance and clarity. [Wikipedia: History of graphic design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_graphic_design).

The Museum für Gestaltung Zürich holds the poster *Piktogramme – München 1972 – Montreal 1976* (concept Otl Aicher; offset, 84 × 59.5 cm, object 33-0114). [eMuseum object 230065](https://www.emuseum.ch/objects/230065).
observed: Each sign is a square panel in one flat color (light blue at the swimming hall, green at the station) with a white figure.
Heads are plain circles detached from the body; limbs and torsos are straight bars with rounded ends.
Bars run only at vertical, horizontal, and 45-degree angles. The runner’s legs and the footballer’s body are built from the same few angles.
The football is a white outline circle, the only outlined shape in the two station panels.
The panels carry no text.
interpretation: The pictograms extend the style from type to symbols: a small set of parts on a fixed geometric grid produces a large family that stays consistent across sports and sites.
borrow: Build icons from a restricted kit: one circle size, one bar width, and only 0°, 45°, and 90° angles.
Separate the head or key element from the body with a gap so shapes read clearly at small size.
Use one flat background color per zone or category, and white for the symbol.

rights.statement: The pictograms remain in copyright. The Commons photographs are CC BY 1.0 and rely on German freedom of panorama; they show a copyrighted design, so no image is stored.

references.title: Muse with Violin screen, Rose Iron Works
references.lede: Paul Fehér’s wrought-iron fire screen for the Rose Iron Works of Cleveland: a gilded violinist in a stepped, silvered frame of arches and stylized leaves on dark blue velvet.
references.summary: Silver-plated steel steps, arches, and leaves on dark blue velvet around a gold figure. Paul Fehér, Cleveland, 1930.

source.label: Cleveland Museum of Art: Muse with Violin Screen, 2020.216

evidence.note: Downloaded the Cleveland Museum of Art web image (900 × 792 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. Read the museum record through the Cleveland Open Access API. No image is stored.

styles.note: The museum itself calls it classic Art Deco; it hits every diagnostic of the rubric: symmetry, steps, repeated stylized ornament, and metal on a deep jewel tone.

context: The museum gives the date 1930, the materials steel, brass, silver and gold plating, and cotton velveteen, and the size 156.2 × 156.2 cm. [Cleveland Museum of Art](https://clevelandart.org/art/2020.216).

The museum text says Martin Rose founded the Rose Iron Works after training in Vienna, hired the Parisian designer Paul Fehér in the 1920s, and describes the screen’s geometric patterning, stylized natural forms, and a central figure reminiscent of Josephine Baker as “the classic motifs of Art Deco design”. [Cleveland Museum of Art](https://clevelandart.org/art/2020.216).

The screen was shown in the museum’s May Show of 1930 and reproduced in *Arts and Decoration* in January 1931, according to the museum’s exhibition and citation lists. [Cleveland Museum of Art](https://clevelandart.org/art/2020.216).
observed: The screen is nearly square, with a tall central panel between two narrower side panels, all framed in hammered silver-colored metal.
The central panel holds a gold nude figure playing a violin, standing on a mound of wavy lines, inside a frame of stacked semicircular arches.
Stepped, right-angled bars in the side panels climb in tiers and carry stylized leaf sprays.
A row of short vertical bars forms a stepped cresting along the top; the feet are grooved blocks.
The metal is set against dark blue velvet, so the silver ornament reads as bright line on a deep ground.
The layout is mirror-symmetrical about the central figure.
interpretation: This is a near-perfect rubric match for the style: symmetry, stepped outlines, arches in regular rhythm, and metal on a dark jewel tone.
It shows the Paris idiom carried to an American industrial metalworks within five years of the 1925 Exposition.
borrow: Frame a central panel with stacked semicircles on each side, like a column of arches.
Use a deep blue ground and draw all ornament in one metallic tone, with a single gold element at the center.

rights.statement: The Cleveland Museum of Art marks the image CC0. Paul Fehér died in 1990, so the design is protected under life-plus-70 terms, and whether it was “published” in the United States in 1930 by exhibition is unclear. Under the skill’s rule a CC0 photograph of a possibly copyrighted screen is not tier A. The lead curator may upgrade it if the museum’s CC0 determination is accepted.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 25 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. A cookie bar covers the bottom 60 pixels of the screenshot.

styles.note: A borderline example: the type and alignment follow the style (one grotesque family, flush left, square buttons, strong scale contrast), but the page uses two accent colors and a full-bleed color photograph. It fails `color.hues`.

observed: The MoMA wordmark is set in heavy black sans-serif at the top left.
The navigation (Visit, Exhibitions and events, Art and artists, Store) is bold black sans-serif, flush left under the wordmark.
At the top right, Membership, a gray Donate button, and a cyan Tickets button have square corners.
