references.title: Neobrutalism components
references.lede: A shadcn/ui-based component set that names the style and turns it into copyable parts.
references.summary: Open-source React and Tailwind components with black outlines and hard offset shadows.

evidence.note: Downloaded the repository’s own README preview image (`public/preview.png`, 1280 × 640) and inspected it. Licence read through the GitHub API on 2026-09-25. The live documentation site was not captured.

styles.note: The project describes itself as neobrutalism-styled, and its preview shows thick black outlines, hard unblurred shadows, and flat fills on every component.

context: The README calls it “a collection of neobrutalism-styled components based on shadcn/ui”, made “for people who want to learn more about neobrutalism style”. Documentation lives at [neobrutalism.dev](https://www.neobrutalism.dev/).
GitHub repository created 25 July 2023. It had about 5,500 stars on 2026-09-25, the most of any repository returned by a GitHub search for “neobrutalism”.
Released under the MIT License, copyright 2023 Samuel Breznjak ([LICENSE](https://github.com/ekmas/neobrutalism-components/blob/main/LICENSE)).
observed: Every card, input, calendar cell, and button has a solid black outline of roughly 2 px.
Cards and buttons cast solid black shadows offset down and to the right, with no blur.
Fills are flat: a pale blue page, white cards, and one saturated blue for primary buttons, the selected date, and the slider track.
Headings are a large, heavy geometric sans-serif; body text is black on white.
Corners are square or very slightly rounded. There are no gradients or transparency.
interpretation: A clean, restrained statement of the web-component grammar of the style: outline plus hard shadow on every surface, one bright accent. It is useful as a baseline because it has almost no illustration or decoration to distract from the system.
borrow: Apply outline and shadow to the component primitives once, so that every composed layout inherits the style. Keep to a single accent color when the content is dense.
next: Capture the live site at neobrutalism.dev and measure border width and shadow offset.

references.title: NeoBrutalism for SwiftUI
references.lede: One SwiftUI modifier that restyles native iOS controls with thick borders and hard shadows.
references.summary: An iOS package that shows the style as a transformation of stock controls.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the README image `docs/media/before-after-light.png` (1980 × 912) and the theme swatch image. Licence read through the GitHub API. The package was not built or run.

styles.note: The package is named for the style and converts native controls into outlined, hard-shadowed blocks with flat fills.

context: The README states: “Add `.neoBrutalism()` at the root and every native control underneath picks up thick borders, hard shadows, and a matching palette.” It lists 30 components and six preset themes, for iOS 17 and later.
GitHub repository created 2 March 2025. MIT License, copyright 2025 Kunal ([LICENSE](https://github.com/rational-kunal/NeoBrutalism/blob/main/LICENSE)).
observed: Left: plain SwiftUI controls with blue link-style text, a thin progress bar, and no borders. Right: the same controls with thick black outlines.
The disclosure row and the Save button fill with flat periwinkle blue and cast a solid black shadow offset down and right.
The progress bar becomes an outlined bar with a flat fill and a hard black divider at the fill edge.
Label type becomes heavier on the transformed side. Corners stay slightly rounded.
interpretation: The before-and-after makes the style legible as a set of deltas: add outline, add hard shadow, fill flat, thicken type. It also shows the style moving from the web into native mobile UI.
borrow: Describe the style as a transformation of default controls. A side-by-side of plain and styled states is a clear way to teach it.

observed: An iPhone mock-up of a course app. The search bar, icon buttons, cards, and “Start” button have thick black outlines.

references.title: Neue Grafik journal
references.lede: The trilingual Zürich journal that stated the style’s principles and printed them as a four-column grid on every cover.
references.summary: Neue Grafik / New Graphic Design / Graphisme actuel, 18 issues, 1958–1965.

source.label: eMuseum, Museum für Gestaltung Zürich: Neue Grafik no. 1

creator.name: Richard Paul Lohse, Josef Müller-Brockmann, Hans Neuburg, and Carlo Vivarelli (editors); cover design Carlo Vivarelli

evidence.note: Downloaded the cover scan of issue 16, July 1963 ([File:Neue Grafik July 1963.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Neue_Grafik_July_1963.jpg), 2953 × 3307 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. Issue 1 data and description read on eMuseum records 23096 and 44032. The image is not stored.

styles.note: The style’s own manifesto and showcase; Wikipedia says it disseminated the style’s tenets and was key to its emergence as a movement.

context: Neue Grafik was a quarterly founded in Zürich on 15 February 1958 by Josef Müller-Brockmann, Hans Neuburg, Richard Paul Lohse, and Carlo Vivarelli. Eighteen issues appeared from 1958 to 1965. [Wikipedia: Neue Grafik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neue_Grafik).

Issue 1, September 1958: letterpress, 28 × 24.8 cm, 75 pages, published and printed by Verlag Otto Walter AG, Olten; cover design Carlo Vivarelli. [eMuseum object 23096](https://www.emuseum.ch/objects/23096), [cover, object 44032](https://www.emuseum.ch/objects/44032).

The eMuseum description of issue 1 notes Akzidenz Grotesk for the headings and Monotype 215 for the texts, and a cover of four columns in which only the issue number changes. [eMuseum object 44032](https://www.emuseum.ch/objects/44032).

Wikipedia notes the journal’s advocacy of photography as a central element of graphic design, and criticism in Zürich that the style was rigid and cold. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neue_Grafik).
observed: Issue 16 cover: the three-language title stacks in three lines of large black grotesque at top left, tightly spaced.
Below the title, the page divides into four columns: contributors’ names in the first, then German, English, and French contents in parallel.
The issue number “16” is the only other large element, set in the first column at the same size as the title.
Everything is black on white and flush left; there are no rules, images, or color.
Large empty bands separate the title, the subtitle row, and the contents.
interpretation: The cover is a table of contents made into a composition. It demonstrates the style’s claim that correct organization of information is itself the design.
The fixed template, with only the number changing, treats the journal as a system rather than a series of individual covers.
borrow: Use parallel columns for parallel languages or versions, aligned line for line.
Design a fixed cover or page template where a single variable, such as a number or date, carries the change.
Let the table of contents be the hero of an index page.
references.related: Published by the editors of [Der Film](ref:der-film-poster-1960) and set in [Akzidenz-Grotesk](ref:akzidenz-grotesk-typeface).

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons marks its cover scan PD-textlogo; this catalogue does not rely on that claim. The journal remains in copyright; no image is stored.

references.title: NN/g, “Neobrutalism: Definition and Best Practices”
references.lede: A usability firm’s definition of the style, with accessibility guidance.
references.summary: Nielsen Norman Group’s 2025 definition: high contrast, blocky layout, bold color, thick borders.

evidence.note: Article text read on 2026-09-25. Byline and date (11 April 2025) are on the page.

styles.note: An authoritative UX source that defines the style under both spellings and lists its traits.

context: Definition: “Neobrutalism (or neubrutalism), an evolution of traditional brutalism, is a visual-design trend defined by high contrast, blocky layouts, bold colors, thick borders, and ‘unpolished’ elements.”
It separates the two: brutalist sites “might use plain HTML elements and limited color palettes” (example: Drudge Report), while neobrutalist designs “are likely to be more colorful and orderly”.

On shadows: “solid, single-color shadows (e.g., a black drop shadow offset by 4px)”. Examples include Gumroad, Figma, 99percentoffsale.com, byooooob.com, cyanbanister.com, dodonut.com, and bieffeforniture.it.
Best practices: meet contrast ratios, limit the palette to 2 or 3 bold colors, pair chunky headings with neutral body fonts, and pad dense shapes with 24 to 32 px.
interpretation: Useful for attestation of the name and for the brutalism versus neobrutalism distinction. Some of its examples lean retro or brutalist rather than outline-and-shadow, so each needs a capture.

rights.statement: © Nielsen Norman Group. Link and quotation only.

references.title: Normandie poster by Cassandre
references.lede: Cassandre’s poster for the French Line shows the liner Normandie head-on: a looming, symmetrical black hull above a band of sea and a stack of centered capitals.
references.summary: A symmetrical frontal view of a liner’s bow in black, white, and red over the name NORMANDIE. Cassandre, 1935.

source.label: Victoria and Albert Museum: Normandie, E.648-2017

evidence.note: Downloaded the V&A image (580 × 900 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. Read the V&A record through its API. The MoMA record could not be read: HTTP 403 to WebFetch, and Claude in Chrome had no permission for moma.org. No image is stored.

styles.note: The best-known poster of the late, streamlined phase of Art Deco, for a liner built as a showcase of French Deco design.

context: The V&A calls the poster “arguably the most iconic work of Cassandre (1901–68)” and says the Normandie entered service with the Compagnie Générale Transatlantique in 1935 and was conceived as a showcase of French Art Deco design. It notes the simplicity and symmetry of the frontal view. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1405126/).
The V&A records colour lithograph on paper backed on cotton, 100.5 × 62.5 cm, printed by Alliance Graphique L. Danel, Paris, 1935. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1405126/).
observed: The bow of the ship fills the upper two-thirds, seen from straight ahead and below, so the hull narrows to a vertical center line.
The hull is black and gray with a red band at the waterline; white superstructure decks flare out on both sides near the top, and a red and black funnel sits above.
The sky is a gradient from deep blue at top to pale blue; a small flock of white birds crosses the lower hull.
A green band of sea runs across below the hull.
“NORMANDIE” is centered in large white sans-serif capitals, followed by centered lines in black and red capitals giving the line and the route Le Havre – Southampton – New-York.
The signature “A.M. CASSANDRE” is at upper right. The composition is symmetrical about the bow.
interpretation: The poster uses Deco symmetry and a stepped, flaring silhouette, but its smooth gradients and machine subject point to the streamline branch the style record lists as a close relative.
The low viewpoint makes the object monumental, the same device as a setback tower seen from the street.
borrow: Center one monumental object on the vertical axis and let it narrow toward the viewer.
Stack centered lines of capitals under the image, changing only color between lines.

rights.statement: Cassandre died in 1968, so the poster is protected in France until 2038. The V&A image is not offered under an open license.

references.title: NYCTA Graphics Standards Manual
references.lede: Unimark’s rulebook for New York’s subway signs: one grotesque, a strict module, and colored route discs.
references.summary: Massimo Vignelli, Bob Noorda, and Unimark International for the New York City Transit Authority, 1966–1970.

source.label: MoMA: New York City Transit Authority Graphics Standards Manual

creator.name: Massimo Vignelli, Bob Noorda, Unimark International Corporation, New York

evidence.note: Read the MoMA record and the OCR text of the scanned manual on the [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/nycta-gs-manual). Page images were not inspected. The stored route disc was inspected; it is a vector reconstruction, not a scan of the manual.

styles.note: A standards manual in the Swiss-trained tradition: one grotesque, sizes and leading fixed on a module, and color used only as a code.

context: MoMA dates the manual 1966–70: lithograph with screenprinted binder, 34.6 × 39.4 × 7.3 cm, gift of the designer, object 374.2004. [MoMA](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/89303).

The manual’s pages carry the line “Unimark International, Consultant Designers” and the date 1970. Its contents list an information tree, sign distribution, type face, type sizes and leading, letter spacing, and color coding. Its reproduction pages give the Standard Medium alphabet. [Internet Archive scan, OCR](https://archive.org/details/nycta-gs-manual).

The color-coding page says each line is shown by a letter or number in white on a colored disc, arranged in alphabetical and then numerical order, from an eight-color code. [Internet Archive scan](https://archive.org/details/nycta-gs-manual).

Wikipedia says Unimark had nearly finished the signage project by 1970, producing this manual, and that Vignelli’s 1972 subway map followed. [Wikipedia: Massimo Vignelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massimo_Vignelli). Standards Manual reissued the manual in 2014 after a Kickstarter campaign. [Standards Manual](https://standardsmanual.com/products/nyctacompactedition).
observed: Stored route disc: a solid blue circle with a white capital A centered in it.
The A is a grotesque capital with a flat apex and horizontal cuts at the foot of each stroke.
The letter is about half the height of the circle, which leaves a wide margin of color around it.
interpretation: The manual moves the style from the poster wall into infrastructure: typographic rules become operating rules that sign makers must follow, and color stops being decoration and becomes data.
borrow: Write type size, leading, and spacing as multiples of one module so every sign or screen shares proportions.
Reserve color for coding (lines, categories, states) and keep type black or white.
Order repeated tokens by a fixed rule, for example letters before numbers.
references.related: The manual specifies Standard Medium, the American name for [Akzidenz-Grotesk](ref:akzidenz-grotesk-typeface); Unimark also used [Helvetica](ref:helvetica-typeface).

images.alt: A New York City Subway route disc: a solid blue circle with a white sans-serif capital A in the center.
images.caption: Route disc for the A service in Standard Medium, extracted with FontForge from the reissued 1970 manual. Credited to the Metropolitan Transportation Authority; public domain (PD-textlogo), trademarked. The blue is the uploader’s color and may not match 1970 practice. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NYCTA-Standard-Medium-A.svg), rendered from SVG to PNG by Wikimedia.

rights.statement: The route disc is marked PD-textlogo (a letter in a circle, below the threshold of originality) on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NYCTA-Standard-Medium-A.svg) and is a trademark of the MTA. The manual itself is not stored; its scan on the Internet Archive has no stated license.

references.title: Offset: Buch und Werbekunst, Bauhaus issue
references.lede: A printing-trade magazine hands its 1926 issue to the Bauhaus, and Joost Schmidt answers with color bands, a black quarter-disc, and concentric rings.
references.summary: Primary-color bands, black circle segment, and heavy sans-serif. Joost Schmidt, cover of Offset no. 7, 1926.

source.label: Harvard Art Museums: Offset: Book and Advertising Art, Vol. 7, Special Issue on the Bauhaus

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the [Commons scan](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Joost_Schmidt_Bauhausheft_7_1926.jpg) (421 × 535 px). The scan is small, so fine print is only partly legible.

styles.note: The primary triad, elementary circle forms, bars of color, and heavy sans-serif type on a Bauhaus special issue.

context: Harvard Art Museums catalogues the cover under Joost Schmidt, 1926, “letterpress and offset lithograph with silver ink on paper,” 30.8 × 23.3 cm, object 2021.170. [Harvard 372865](https://harvardartmuseums.org/collections/object/372865).

Letterform Archive lists it as Offset: Buch und Werbekunst, Bauhaus-Heft, vol. 3, no. 7, Leipzig, 1926, with Joost Schmidt as cover designer. [Letterform Archive](https://exhibitions.letterformarchive.org/bauhaus/artworks/offset-book-and-advertising-art-bauhaus-issue). MoMA also holds a copy. [MoMA 130203](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/130203).
observed: A yellow vertical band runs down the left edge; a gray field fills the right side.
A large black circle segment, with a stippled yellow edge, fills the upper middle.
Concentric rings in red, blue, yellow, and black spread from a small blue and white center at upper right.
“OFFSET” is set in very heavy red sans-serif capitals; “BUCH UND WERBEKUNST” is in white capitals on a blue band; “HEFT 7” and “1926” are on a black and a white band below.
Small vertical type at the right edge reads “BAUHAUS-HEFT” and credits the design to Joost Schmidt, Bauhaus in Dessau.
interpretation: The cover uses every item of the Bauhaus rubric at once: red, yellow, and blue as flat areas, circles as composition elements, heavy sans-serif, and bands that divide the page.
The concentric rings add optical movement, which links Schmidt’s cover to Bauhaus color and form teaching.
borrow: Stack the masthead on horizontal color bands of different heights.
Use one large circle segment as the main image instead of a picture.

images.alt: Magazine cover: a yellow band at left, a large black circle segment, concentric red, blue, and yellow rings at upper right, and a gray field; below, the word Offset in heavy red capitals over blue, black, and white bands reading Buch und Werbekunst, Heft 7, 1926.
images.caption: Joost Schmidt, cover of Offset: Buch und Werbekunst, no. 7 (Bauhaus issue), 1926. Scan on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Joost_Schmidt_Bauhausheft_7_1926.jpg), public domain.

rights.statement: Marked public domain on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Joost_Schmidt_Bauhausheft_7_1926.jpg). Joost Schmidt died in 1948, and the issue was published in 1926. Harvard’s record still shows “© Joost Schmidt / Artists Rights Society”; Bauhaus Kooperation marks Schmidt’s 1923 poster as public domain since 2018.

references.title: Poste Italiane Agenzia 62, Rome
references.lede: A “post office of the future” with backlit frosted glass, curved white columns, cool blue light, and touch screens.
references.summary: Backlit glass, curved white forms, and blue light in a post office interior. Massimo Iosa Ghini, 2007.

source.label: Archilovers: Poste Italiane design Massimo Iosa Ghini

evidence.note: Inspected three project photographs on the Archilovers page in scratchpad copies (self-service area, payment kiosks, ATM wall). Not stored.

styles.note: Avcı names it “one of the successful examples” of Frutiger Aero’s color and texture effects in a physical interior.

context: Agenzia 62 of Poste Italiane, inside the Sapienza university campus in Rome, was designed by Massimo Iosa Ghini’s studio as the first “new generation” post office, with new signage, interactive panels, and a self-service area. Archilovers lists the project year as 2007. [Archilovers](https://www.archilovers.com/projects/16766/poste-italiane-design-massimo-iosa-ghini.html); [Domus, 2008](https://www.domusweb.it/it/notizie/2008/10/27/le-poste-italiane-si-rinnovano.html).

Avcı describes “transparent and glossy surfaces, with curved forms throughout the space,” concealed LED lighting, curved glass panels with circular halftone patterns, and the brand colors blue, yellow, and green. [Avcı 2024, “Physical reflections of digital aesthetics”](https://doi.org/10.17932/IAU.EJNM.25480200.2024/ejnm_v8i3003), p. 471.
observed: Walls are frosted glass panels lit from behind in pale cyan and white.
White columns and wall edges are molded into soft, wavy curves.
Round recessed ceiling lights and a long oval light cove glow over a pale floor.
Yellow self-service kiosks with blue screens and a tall blue sign panel give saturated accents against white and cyan.
interpretation: The interior translates interface glass into building materials: backlit translucent panels play the part of Aero glass, and touch screens make the link to software literal.
borrow: On screen, a translucent panel lit from behind (white-to-cyan glow, no hard border) reads like this backlit glass.
Let one saturated brand color act as an accent on an otherwise white and cyan field.

rights.statement: Photographs on Archilovers belong to their authors or the studio; the design belongs to its owners. No image is stored here.

references.title: Poster for the 1923 Bauhaus exhibition
references.lede: Joost Schmidt’s railway-station poster joins the school’s name, the dates, and the signet into one diagonal figure of circles, squares, and bars.
references.summary: Red, black, and gray circles and rectangles on a diagonal cross. Joost Schmidt, Weimar, 1923.

source.label: Bauhaus Kooperation: Plakat zur Bauhaus-Ausstellung in Weimar 1923

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Bauhaus-Archiv image published by Bauhaus Kooperation (710 × 1016 px). This copy has the later overprint that moves the opening to 15 August. Also compared the smaller [Commons copy](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Joost_Schmidt_Bauhausausstellung_1923.jpg), which shows the first state with “Juli–Sept”.

styles.note: A canonical Bauhaus poster: elementary circles and rectangles, heavy bars, a strong diagonal, and flat red and black.

context: Schmidt made the design for a competition. It is a cross of circles and squares set on the diagonal, and it contains Oskar Schlemmer’s Bauhaus signet, which the competition brief required. [Bauhaus Kooperation](https://bauhauskooperation.de/wissen/das-bauhaus/werke/graphische-druckerei/plakat-zur-bauhaus-ausstellung-in-weimar-1923).

The first version advertised the exhibition in 120 German railway stations with the dates July to September. A sticker later updated the dates. [Bauhaus Kooperation](https://bauhauskooperation.de/wissen/das-bauhaus/werke/graphische-druckerei/plakat-zur-bauhaus-ausstellung-in-weimar-1923).
The Museum of Modern Art holds a copy as “Staatliches Bauhaus Ausstellung,” 1923. [MoMA 6235](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/6235).
observed: A red ring at upper left and a large black half-disc at lower right sit at the ends of a thick black diagonal band.
Rectangles in black, red, and stippled gray overlap at right angles along the band.
“STAATLICHES BAUHAUS” runs above the ring; “AUSSTELLUNG”, “WEIMAR”, and “1923” follow the diagonal.
The capitals are hand-drawn and angular, built from straight strokes and small arcs.
A small version of the Schlemmer signet sits inside the red ring.
A pink overprint strip reads “Eröffnung verschoben auf 15. Aug – 30. Sept”.
The ground is unprinted off-white paper. Wide empty margins surround the central figure.
interpretation: The poster shows the change from the expressionist early Bauhaus to constructive geometry. Type and shapes form one system: the words follow the same diagonal as the bars.
The palette is red, black, and gray, not the full primary triad. This reduced red-and-black version is common in Bauhaus print work.
borrow: Build a heading and its shapes into one diagonal figure, and let the words follow the edges of the shapes.
Use one saturated accent with black and a textured gray, and leave wide margins of plain ground.

images.alt: Poster on off-white paper: a red ring and a large black half-disc joined by a black diagonal band with overlapping red, black, and gray rectangles. The words Staatliches Bauhaus, Ausstellung, Weimar, and 1923 follow the shapes, and a pink strip gives the new opening date, 15 August.
images.caption: Joost Schmidt, poster for the 1923 Bauhaus exhibition, copy with the date overprint. Bauhaus-Archiv Berlin, image from [Bauhaus Kooperation](https://bauhauskooperation.de/wissen/das-bauhaus/werke/graphische-druckerei/plakat-zur-bauhaus-ausstellung-in-weimar-1923), marked public domain.

rights.statement: Bauhaus Kooperation credits the image “Bauhaus-Archiv Berlin / gemeinfrei / abgelaufen 2018” (public domain, term expired 2018). Joost Schmidt died in 1948. The poster was published in 1923, so it is also in the public domain in the United States.

references.title: RetroUI (neobrutalism/neobrutalism)
references.lede: A React and Tailwind library published under the name NeoBrutalism, now branded RetroUI.
references.summary: Component library whose banner mixes hard-shadowed display type with retro window frames.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the README banner `public/banner.png` (1200 × 630). Licence read through the GitHub API. The live sites were not captured.

styles.note: The repository is published as a NeoBrutalism library, and its banner uses outlined blocks, hard shadows, and flat yellow fills.

context: The GitHub description reads “A NeoBrutalism styled React + TailwindCSS UI library”. The README heading is “Retro UI”, with documentation at [retroui.dev](https://retroui.dev/docs). On 2026-09-25 the page title of retroui.dev began “NeoBrutalism — Retro UI components for React”.
Repository created 31 August 2024 under the GitHub organization “NeoBrutalism.com”. MIT License, copyright 2024 Arif Hossain.
observed: Heavy black condensed display type with a hard white-and-black offset, reading “Not every website has to look the same!”.
Mock browser windows with thick black frames, yellow title bars, and three-dot controls.
Cards inside the mock pages have black outlines and flat pastel or yellow fills.
Cartoon stickers (a yellow bird, cartoon eyes) have heavy black outlines.

rights.statement: The repository is MIT-licensed, but the banner includes third-party logos (Figma, Tailwind CSS, React), so it is not stored here.

references.title: Segoe UI typeface
references.lede: The humanist sans-serif that actually set the text of Vista and Windows 7, and the typeface behind the “Frutiger” in the name.
references.summary: Rounded humanist sans-serif of the Aero interfaces. Monotype for Microsoft, first shipped with Windows Vista.
references.made: Segoe designed c. 2000 at Agfa Monotype; Segoe UI first introduced with Windows Vista

evidence.note: Inspected [File:Segoe UI Revision Differences.png](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Segoe_UI_Revision_Differences.png) (1200 × 650, PD-font) and stored it. Also saw Segoe UI in the Vista and Windows 7 screenshots inspected for [Windows Vista](ref:windows-vista-aero-interface) and [Windows 7](ref:windows-7-aero-interface).

styles.note: Segoe UI is the humanist interface type of Windows Aero, and CARI links it to Frutiger in the style’s name.

context: Segoe was designed by Steve Matteson at Agfa Monotype and licensed to Microsoft. Segoe UI “was first introduced with Windows Vista” and replaced Tahoma as the interface font; Light and Semibold weights came with Windows 7. [Wikipedia: Segoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Segoe).

In 2004 Linotype protested Microsoft’s EU design registration of Segoe, citing its similarity to Frutiger; the EU revoked the registration. Microsoft states that Segoe was not derived from Frutiger. [Wikipedia: Segoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Segoe).
CARI says Frutiger “originally inspired Vista’s default font (Segoe UI).” [CARI: Frutiger Aero](https://cari.institute/aesthetics/frutiger-aero). This is CARI’s claim; Microsoft disputes derivation.
In October 2011 the letters I and Q and several figures were redrawn; I, Q, and 1 became closer to Frutiger. [Wikipedia: Segoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Segoe).
observed: The top line (Vista and Windows 7 version) shows “IQ124578” with round, open forms; the I has serifs, the 1 has a foot, and the Q tail sweeps down and out to the right.
The bottom line (2011 revision) has a plain I, a 1 without a foot, and a short straight Q tail; the 2, 4, 5, 7, and 8 are also redrawn.
In the Vista and Windows 7 screenshots, menu and window text is set in small, even, humanist sans-serif.
interpretation: If a catalogue specimen needs “the” Frutiger Aero typeface, Segoe UI is the documented interface face; Frutiger names the tradition. Both are humanist and open.
borrow: Use Segoe UI (or a free humanist substitute) at small, regular weights for body and control labels; keep headings light rather than heavy.

references.title: Staatliches Bauhaus in Weimar 1919–1923
references.lede: The first survey of the school, published for the 1923 exhibition: Moholy-Nagy’s layout and Bayer’s cover put the Bauhaus idea into print.
references.summary: Exhibition book with a red-and-black title page by László Moholy-Nagy and a red-and-blue cover by Herbert Bayer, 1923.

source.label: The Met: “Staatliches Bauhaus in Weimar 1919-1923” Book

creator.name: László Moholy-Nagy (layout), Herbert Bayer (cover); edited by Walter Gropius

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the [title page scan](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:StaatlichesBauhausTitelseite.jpg) and the [front cover scan](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:StaatlichesBauhaus_Vorderdeckel.jpg) from Wikimedia Commons, both photographed by Tobias Adam from the Weimar university library copy. Only the title page is stored.

styles.note: A key Bauhaus publication: sans-serif capitals, a giant red initial, vertical and horizontal type, and asymmetric composition.

context: The Met lists the book under Walter Gropius, 1923, “printed halftone and lithographic printing on paper,” 24.6 × 25.3 cm, accession 2001.392. [The Met 492179](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/492179).

MoMA credits the design to Herbert Bayer and László Moholy-Nagy. [MoMA 7567](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/7567). The Commons scans credit the title page to Moholy-Nagy and the front cover to Bayer. [Title page](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:StaatlichesBauhausTitelseite.jpg), [cover](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:StaatlichesBauhaus_Vorderdeckel.jpg).

Bauhaus Kooperation describes the book as the catalogue that accompanied the first public exhibition of the school in 1923. [Bauhaus Kooperation](https://bauhauskooperation.de/en/knowledge/publications/publikationen-zum-bauhaus/staatliches-bauhaus-weimar-1919-1923).
observed: Title page: a very tall red capital B fills the left side and serves as the first letter of the red word “AUHAUS”.
“STAATLICHES” is set in black outline capitals filled with horizontal stripes; “WEIMAR” runs vertically in the same striped letters.
“1919 1923” is set in heavy black sans-serif figures beside the vertical word.
“BAUHAUSVERLAG” runs vertically and meets “WEIMAR-MÜNCHEN” at a right angle, like a bracket.
Cover (not stored): condensed capitals in alternating red and blue blocks fill a black ground edge to edge.
interpretation: The title page treats letters as building parts: one huge initial, words turned 90 degrees, and type that locks into right angles. It is an early example of the “new typography” that Moholy-Nagy promoted.
The red-and-black palette with textured letter fills reads as Bauhaus without any circles or triangles.
borrow: Use one oversized initial as a structural element and hang the rest of the title from it.
Rotate a secondary line 90 degrees to make an L-shaped bracket with a horizontal line.

images.alt: Title page on tan paper: a huge red B forms the start of the red word Bauhaus; Staatliches is in black striped capitals across the top, Weimar runs vertically in striped letters, and 1919 1923 is in heavy black figures.
images.caption: Title page of Staatliches Bauhaus in Weimar 1919–1923, layout by László Moholy-Nagy. Photograph by Tobias Adam on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:StaatlichesBauhausTitelseite.jpg), public domain.

rights.statement: The stored title page is marked public domain on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:StaatlichesBauhausTitelseite.jpg). Moholy-Nagy died in 1946, and the book was published in 1923. The Bayer cover is not stored: its Commons photograph is CC BY-SA 4.0, and Bayer died in 1985, so the design is still protected outside the United States.

references.title: Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam website
references.lede: The museum’s home page stacks its name and its programme as full-width lines of very large grotesque capitals between heavy black rules.
references.summary: Huge black grotesque capitals in full-width bands between heavy rules, with one flat green button.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 25 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. A cookie notice covers part of the lower right quarter of the screenshot.

styles.note: A clear example: grotesque type at extreme scale, flush left, in black and white with one flat accent, organized in horizontal bands. It passes every fingerprint metric.

observed: The word STEDELIJK fills the full width of the page in very large black grotesque capitals.
A tilted yellow sticker with the word “Unbubble” in a heavy rounded display face overlaps the last letters of the name.
Below it, “MUSEUM OF MODERN AND CONTEMPORARY ART AND DESIGN” is set in one line of smaller capitals.
Heavy black horizontal rules divide the page into bands. Each band holds one line of large capitals, such as “WHAT’S ON: EXHIBITIONS &” and “YAYOI KUSAMA”, cut off at the right edge.
One small square photograph sits inside a band next to the word NEW.
The only flat color in the interface is a bright green “Book ticket” button at the top right.
interpretation: The measurement finds one grotesque family (Union) for 98% of the text, square corners, no shadows, two CSS colors, a size range of 3.47, and 52% uppercase text.
The yellow sticker is an exhibition campaign placed on top of the identity, not part of the grid. It is the one element that breaks the style.
borrow: Treat a list of exhibitions as a stack of full-width type bands separated by heavy rules.
Keep one accent color for the one action that matters (here, tickets).

references.title: Super lamp
references.lede: Martine Bedin’s table lamp on wheels: a blue half-disc with six bulbs in colored collars.
references.summary: Bedin’s wheeled half-circle lamp with bulbs in six colored sockets; first Memphis show, 1981.
references.made: ca. 1977 and 1981, as the V&A records them; the V&A example is the 1981 prototype

evidence.note: Downloaded the museum’s published image (843 px wide) from [the V&A IIIF server](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1177310/) to a private scratchpad and inspected it with the Read tool on 2026-09-25. No image is stored in the catalogue.

styles.note: Shown at the first Memphis exhibition in 1981; the V&A calls it iconic.

context: The V&A says the Super lamp was among Bedin’s contributions to the first Memphis year (1981). Its example is the initial prototype, shown at the first Memphis exhibition at the gallery Arc 74 in 1981. [V&A record](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1177310/).

The physical description: painted sheet steel, two stamped semicircular halves painted blue, six light sockets in steel collars of different colors along the curve, and four steel wheels with rubber tyres. [V&A record](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1177310/).
The V&A notes that Bedin worked mainly on lighting and graphic design for Memphis and introduced Nathalie Du Pasquier to the group. [V&A record](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1177310/).
observed: The body is a glossy navy half-circle standing on its flat edge.
Six bare bulbs stick out along the curve in collars of red, lime, yellow, light blue, green, and pink.
Four black rubber wheels make it look like a pull toy.
The background is plain white, so the colors read as separate dots around the arc.
interpretation: The lamp combines a pull toy, a rainbow, and a sunrise. The ring of colored collars on one dark shape is a small version of the Memphis palette.
borrow: Place a row of small, differently colored elements along one bold dark curve.
Add toy cues such as wheels or handles to domestic objects or interface elements.

rights.statement: The V&A image is credited ©Victoria and Albert Museum, London/Martine Bedin. No image is stored.

references.title: Tawaraya colour tests
references.lede: Masanori Umeda’s drawing for Tawaraya, the boxing-ring bed shown at the first Memphis exhibition.
references.summary: Umeda’s 1981 colour test: a boxing-ring bed with striped base and pink ropes.

source.label: M+, Hong Kong: Colour tests, Tawaraya (ring), bed (CA28/6/2)

evidence.note: Downloaded the museum’s published image (705 × 1000 px) from [M+](https://www.mplus.org.hk/en/collection/objects/colour-tests-tawaraya-ring-bed-ca28-6-2/) to a private scratchpad and inspected it with the Read tool on 2026-09-25. No image is stored in the catalogue. The file holds seven items; only the first image was inspected. The finished bed itself was not seen.

styles.note: A design drawing for one of the defining pieces of the first Memphis exhibition.

context: M+ describes the file as drawings that test colour patterns for the design, some printed with the words “banchetto, dialogo, godimento, sapienza”. Ink on paper, May 1981, seven items. [M+ record](https://www.mplus.org.hk/en/collection/objects/colour-tests-tawaraya-ring-bed-ca28-6-2/).

An M+ magazine article by curator Ikko Yokoyama (2021) says Tawaraya was shown at the first Memphis exhibition in Milan on 18 September 1981. It describes a boxing ring with black-and-white striped edges, a tatami centre, multicoloured ropes, and lamps on four posts, 280 × 280 × 120 cm. [M+ Magazine](https://www.mplus.org.hk/en/magazine/tawaraya/).

The same article says Sottsass named it after a Kyoto ryokan, and that Fabio Cirifino photographed the Memphis designers sitting in it in 1981. [M+ Magazine](https://www.mplus.org.hk/en/magazine/tawaraya/).
observed: An isometric drawing shows a square ring on a base of heavy black-and-white vertical stripes.
Pink ropes run between four posts; each post ends in a small globe on a coiled stem.
Inside are pale tatami panels, cushions tinted in soft rainbow gradients, and a small red square tray.
Four large kanji and the Italian words banchetto, dialogo, godimento, and sapienza are placed at the corners.
Handwritten at the bottom: “Mobili ‘4 ½’ Maggio 81 Umeda”.
interpretation: The drawing combines Memphis’s black-and-white stripes with a sport object and a Japanese room type. It shows the group’s method of combining references from unrelated contexts.
borrow: Use a heavy black-and-white striped band as a base or frame, with light pastel color inside.
Draw in isometric to present an object as a small stage or a toy.

rights.statement: M+ states “Copyright: © Masanori Umeda”. No image is stored.

references.title: The Swiss Grid exhibition website
references.lede: Poster House’s microsite for its Swiss Grid exhibition opens with the title in huge white Akzidenz-Grotesk on black.
references.summary: The words The Swiss Grid in huge white grotesque on black, with the museum’s name turned vertically at the edges.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 25 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: A borderline example: the type (Akzidenz-Grotesk, extreme scale, black and white) belongs to the style, but the first viewport is one centered title block, which the rubric counts against it. The site is about the style, which is not evidence that it uses it. It passes every fingerprint metric because the lines are left-aligned inside a centered block (see the style page).

observed: The page is black.
The title “The Swiss Grid” fills most of the screen in three lines of very large white grotesque type. The block of three lines sits in the middle of the page.
The word POSTER runs vertically down the top left edge and HOUSE runs vertically up the bottom right edge, in heavy white capitals.
A thin eye icon and a three-line menu icon sit at the top right. A thin down arrow sits at the bottom center.

references.title: Typographie, by Emil Ruder
references.lede: The Basel school’s typography textbook, in three languages, with a cover built from blocks of letters.
references.summary: Emil Ruder, Verlag Niggli, 1967. A trilingual design textbook that spread the Swiss style.

source.label: eMuseum, Museum für Gestaltung Zürich: L RUDE 1

evidence.note: Downloaded a photograph of the dust jacket ([File:Обложка книги Эмиля Рудера «Typographie».jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%D0%9E%D0%B1%D0%BB%D0%BE%D0%B6%D0%BA%D0%B0_%D0%BA%D0%BD%D0%B8%D0%B3%D0%B8_%D0%AD%D0%BC%D0%B8%D0%BB%D1%8F_%D0%A0%D1%83%D0%B4%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%B0_%C2%ABTypographie%C2%BB.jpg), 884 × 907 px, CC BY-SA 4.0) to a scratch folder and inspected it. Interior pages were not seen. The image is not stored.

styles.note: Wikipedia says the book helped spread the Swiss style and became a basic text in design programmes in Europe and North America.

context: *Typographie: Ein Gestaltungslehrbuch*, 1967 (1st edition; 6th edition 1996). Offset, 28 × 22.3 cm, 220 pages. Published by Verlag Niggli AG, Sulgen; printed by Heer Druck AG. Photography by Werner Blaser, André Gürtler, and Armin Hofmann. [eMuseum object 36839](https://www.emuseum.ch/objects/36839).

Ruder, born in Zürich in 1914, trained as a typesetter in Basel. The book was published in German, English, and French by Arthur Niggli in 1967. [Wikipedia: Emil Ruder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emil_Ruder).

Ruder also designed covers of *Typographische Monatsblätter*, including the January 1961 issue devoted to [Univers](ref:univers-typeface). [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:TM_Typographische_Monatsbl%C3%A4tter_1961_01.jpg).
observed: The square jacket is white with a large black field in which the letters of TYPOGRAPHIE appear white, each in its own black rectangle.
A very large T fills the right two thirds; Y fills a box above the smaller boxes; PO, GRA, and PHIE sit in a grid of small squares at lower left.
The small letters are mirrored, as if seen from the back of metal type.
Author and title appear once more in small plain type at top right, flush with the black field’s right edge.
There is no color: only black and white.
interpretation: The cover teaches the book’s lesson: one word divided into modules of different sizes, held by a grid. The mirrored letters point back to the composing room, where Ruder trained.
borrow: Break one word into grid cells of unequal size to create hierarchy inside a single element.
Pair a very large display letter with a small, plain title line placed at an edge.

rights.statement: The book and its cover remain in copyright. The Commons photograph is CC BY-SA 4.0 but shows a copyrighted cover, so no image is stored.

references.title: Univers typeface
references.lede: Adrian Frutiger’s 1957 grotesque, planned from the start as one matched system of weights and widths.
references.summary: Adrian Frutiger for Deberny & Peignot, 1957. A numbered, matched family of neo-grotesque styles.

evidence.note: Inspected and stored the public-domain digital specimen [File:Univers Specimen.svg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Univers_Specimen.svg), rendered by Wikimedia at 960 px.

styles.note: A neo-grotesque built as a consistent family; Wikipedia links its matched range to the Swiss-style wish for neutral type.

context: Univers was designed by Adrian Frutiger and released by Deberny & Peignot in 1957. It was available from launch in a wide range of weights and widths, and its marketing referred to the periodic table. [Wikipedia: Univers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Univers).

Wikipedia says the matched range allowed a whole document to be set in one consistent sans-serif, which suited Swiss-style practitioners who wanted neutral type. The design was planned for phototypesetting but also cast in metal. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Univers).

Emil Ruder devoted the January 1961 issue of *Typographische Monatsblätter* to Univers, according to its [Commons file description](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:TM_Typographische_Monatsbl%C3%A4tter_1961_01.jpg). See [Typographie](ref:typographie-emil-ruder-1967).
observed: Stroke ends are cut horizontally, and curves thin slightly where they join stems, for example in the n and the a.
The large white a has a straight, vertical stem and a bowl that meets it with a visible taper.
The italic is an oblique form of the roman, not a separate cursive design.
The bold “Ausstellung” in red keeps the same proportions as the regular letters.
interpretation: Univers makes the style’s systematic thinking visible inside the type family itself: weights and widths are coordinates in a grid, not separate faces with their own characters.
borrow: Define type styles as a numbered system (weight × width) and use only the cells you need. It keeps hierarchy consistent across a long document.
Related: Frutiger’s later humanist design, [Frutiger](ref:frutiger-typeface-1976).

images.alt: Type specimen of Univers: the name in dark gray, “Aa Ee Rr” in roman and oblique, a large white lowercase a, the word “Ausstellung” in bold red, and the lowercase alphabet and figures on a red band.
images.caption: Univers specimen by Sherbyte, 2010, released into the public domain. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Univers_Specimen.svg), rendered from SVG to PNG by Wikimedia.

rights.statement: Released into the public domain by its author (PD-self, Sherbyte) on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Univers_Specimen.svg). Letterform designs are not copyrightable in the United States. Univers is a trademark; the name and font software belong to their owners.

references.title: Vase by Jean Dunand
references.lede: Jean Dunand’s dark metal vase covered in a dense all-over pattern of inlaid silver zigzags, meanders, and sunbursts.
references.summary: Dark copper vase with silver inlaid zigzags, step patterns, and small suns. Jean Dunand, Paris, c. 1925.

evidence.note: Downloaded the Art Institute of Chicago IIIF image (843 × 1303 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. Read the record through the AIC API. No image is stored.

styles.note: Dunand was a leading Art Deco metalworker and lacquerer; this vase is classified Art Deco by the museum and uses the style’s zigzag and stepped ornament.

context: The Art Institute records the vase as c. 1925, copper and silver inlay, 28.6 × 12.7 cm, by Jean Dunand (French, 1877–1942), Paris. Style: Art Deco. Credit: Gift of Arthur T. Aldis and Russell Tyson. [Art Institute of Chicago](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/18896/vase).
The AIC API marks the object as not in the public domain. [AIC API](https://api.artic.edu/api/v1/artworks/18896).
observed: The vase is a tall ovoid with a narrow flared neck; the metal is dark gray-brown with a soft sheen.
Thin lighter lines of inlay cover the whole surface in a dense pattern of zigzags, stepped meanders, concentric arcs, and small star or sun shapes.
The pattern is irregular and all-over, not arranged in bands or panels.
There is no color other than the dark ground and the lighter inlay.
interpretation: The inlay is a catalogue of Deco motifs in one object: zigzag, step, arc, and sunburst, drawn as light line on a dark metal ground.
Its free, all-over layout is looser than the symmetrical Deco rubric; it shows the influence of African and Cubist pattern on French decorative art.
borrow: Fill a dark surface with thin light-line zigzags and steps as a texture.
Limit the palette to one dark metal ground and one lighter line color.

rights.statement: The Art Institute does not mark the image public domain. Jean Dunand died in 1942, so the design is probably in the public domain in France, but the source does not state an open license for the image.

references.title: Victoria vase
references.lede: Marco Zanini’s porcelain vase for Memphis: a ribbed lilac column with a blue-and-yellow fan on top.
references.summary: Zanini’s 1982 Memphis vase: stacked lilac rings under a scalloped two-color fan.

source.label: Art Institute of Chicago: Victoria Vase (1986.411a)

creator.name: Marco Zanini; made by Memphis S.R.L.

evidence.note: Downloaded the museum’s published image (843 px wide) from [the Art Institute of Chicago IIIF server](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/105454) to a private scratchpad and inspected it with the Read tool on 2026-09-25. No image is stored in the catalogue.

styles.note: Made by Memphis S.R.L., and its stacked forms and clashing colors match the group’s object language.

context: The Art Institute lists the vase as designed by Marco Zanini and made by Memphis S.R.L., Milan, 1982; porcelain with enamel decoration, 64.8 cm high. It was purchased from Memphis s.r.l. [AIC record](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/105454).
The record gives separate dimensions for a flat top piece, 43.5 × 35.9 × 1.4 cm. [AIC record](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/105454).
observed: The lower body is a lilac column of stacked discs and ridged, bead-like swellings on a round foot.
A flat quarter-circle sits upright on top, split on the diagonal into deep blue and yellow.
The yellow half has a scalloped outer edge; the blue half has a smooth curve.
All surfaces are glossy and flat in color, without pattern.
interpretation: The vase stacks unrelated forms, a turned column and a flat cut-out, and gives them unrelated colors. This joining of parts that do not match is typical of Memphis objects.
borrow: Top a solid, repetitive base with one flat, cut-out shape in contrasting colors.
Use a scalloped or wavy edge against a straight or smooth one.

rights.statement: AIC marks the object as not public domain. No image is stored.

references.title: View of an Interior
references.lede: George Sowden’s black-and-white lithograph of a Memphis room in which every surface carries a pattern.
references.summary: Sowden’s 1983 lithograph: a patterned interior with his Memphis furniture.

evidence.note: Downloaded the museum’s published image (843 px wide) from [the V&A IIIF server](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1194268/) to a private scratchpad and inspected it with the Read tool on 2026-09-25. No image is stored in the catalogue.

styles.note: A print by a Memphis founder that shows the group’s idea of total surface pattern.

context: The V&A describes three 1983 lithographs by George Sowden, the only British member of Memphis. It says they are unusual as graphic designs from the group and show interiors “saturated with pattern on every surface”. [V&A record](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1194268/).

The prints show furniture Sowden designed for Memphis, such as the Savoy vitrine, Pierre table, d’Antibe cabinet, and Oberoi armchair. They also show patterns he developed for laminates and upholstery with Nathalie Du Pasquier. [V&A record](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1194268/).
observed: The print is pure black and white; there is no gray.
The walls carry a dense squiggle pattern, and the floor is irregular cobbles.
Furniture surfaces carry more patterns: crazed-paving blocks, confetti triangles, and black-and-white stripes.
Open double doors frame a detailed engraving of a Gothic or Renaissance facade.
Signed in pencil “George J. Sowden Milano 1983”, numbered 66/99.
interpretation: With color removed, the print shows that Memphis patterns are drawn as marks on a field. Many different marks can sit side by side because they share one weight of black.
It shows the black-and-white foil that the [Memphis style](style:memphis) uses under its colors.
borrow: Build a pattern library in black on white first, then add color.
Give each plane of a scene a different pattern, and keep line weight constant so they read as one family.

references.title: Whitney Museum of American Art website
references.lede: The museum’s home page uses its responsive W, a zigzag line drawn across the page, above bold grotesque navigation between thin rules.
references.summary: A thin zigzag W across the top, bold black grotesque capitals for navigation, and artworks in a two-column grid.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 25 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. A cookie notice covers part of the lower left of the screenshot.

styles.note: A clear example in the interface: one grotesque family, flush-left capitals, thin rules, square outlined buttons, and only black, white, and gray. The color on the page comes from the artworks. It passes every fingerprint metric.

context: The Whitney’s graphic identity, the “responsive W”, was designed by Experimental Jetset in 2013 ([studio archive](https://www.jetset.nl/archive/whitney-museum-identity)). The studio has not been confirmed as the designer of the current website.
observed: A thin black zigzag line crosses the full width of the page and forms a large W.
The word WHITNEY sits inside the first valley of the zigzag in heavy black capitals.
“Open today: 10:30 am–10 pm” and two square outlined buttons, BOOK TICKETS and BECOME A MEMBER, sit at the right, above a thin rule.
The navigation (VISIT, WHAT’S ON, ART & ARTISTS, LEARN, SHOP) is set in large bold black capitals, flush left, between two thin rules.
Below, a wide image of a colorful painting and a narrower image of a hot dog with ketchup sit in two columns.
The caption “ALEX DA CORTE: HOT DOG WITH KETCHUP” is set in bold capitals, the first line black and the second gray.
interpretation: The measurement finds only Neue Haas Grotesk (haas-grotesk-text and haas-grotesk-sign), square corners, no shadows, two CSS colors, and a size range of 3.25.
The zigzag is the identity’s one graphic form, and it is drawn with a thin line, not filled. This follows the style’s preference for simple geometric forms over illustration.
borrow: Use one thin geometric line as the identity mark, and let type and rules do the rest of the work.

references.title: Wii Menu
references.lede: Nintendo’s console home screen: a grid of rounded “channel” tiles on white, with pale-blue curves and round glossy buttons.
references.summary: Rounded white channel tiles and pale-blue curves. Nintendo Wii system menu, 2006.

creator.name: Nintendo (development led by Takashi Aoyama, Integrated Research & Development Division)

references.made: 2006 (the Wii launched in the United States on November 19, 2006)

evidence.note: Inspected the non-free 420 × 236 screenshot [File:Wiimen.png](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wiimen.png) (Wii Menu after a system update) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored. The console was not used.

styles.note: Wikipedia and Avcı both name the Wii among the consoles that used the style; the menu shows its white, rounded, pale-blue side.

context: The Wii Menu was the Wii’s main interface. Development was led by Takashi Aoyama; the “channels” concept presented applications like a row of televisions in an electronics shop. The Wii launched with six channels, including the Forecast and News channels. [Wikipedia: Wii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#Wii_Menu).

Wikipedia names “video game consoles such as the Wii” among the media that used Frutiger Aero. [Wikipedia: Frutiger Aero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frutiger_Aero). Avcı lists the Nintendo Wii with the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 as examples. [Avcı 2024, “Physical reflections of digital aesthetics”](https://doi.org/10.17932/IAU.EJNM.25480200.2024/ejnm_v8i3003), p. 461.

Dazed describes parents playing “virtual tennis on Wii Sports” as part of the era’s setting. [Holliday, Dazed, 2023](https://www.dazeddigital.com/life-culture/article/58103/1/what-is-frutiger-aero-aesthetic-tiktok-msn-messenger-windows-vista-noughties).
observed: Twelve rounded-rectangle tiles fill a light gray-white grid; empty tiles carry a faint embossed “Wii” mark.
The Forecast Channel tile is a saturated blue gradient; the News Channel tile is green with a globe.
A curved, pale-blue line separates the grid from a lower bar that holds a thin digital clock and the date.
Two round buttons sit at the lower corners: a “Wii” button and a mail envelope, each with a pale-blue rim.
interpretation: This is Frutiger Aero at its lightest: white and pale blue instead of deep glass, with gloss reduced to rims and tiles. It shows that the style can be calm and domestic, not only showy.
borrow: Use a white field with one curved pale-blue divider line to separate content from controls.
Make secondary actions round buttons with a colored rim and a soft inner highlight.

references.title: Windows 7 Aero interface and default wallpaper
references.lede: The refined, brighter Aero of 2009, with a glowing Windows logo, bubbles, grass, and a butterfly on a blue field.
references.summary: Blue glass taskbar, glossy Start orb, and a wallpaper of light, bubbles, and grass. Windows 7, 2009.

evidence.note: Inspected the non-free 640 × 480 screenshot [File:Windows 7 SP1 screenshot.png](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Windows_7_SP1_screenshot.png) (Windows 7 Ultimate with the Start menu open) and the 425 × 235 crop [File:Aero Example.png](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aero_Example.png) in scratchpad copies. Not stored.

styles.note: Windows 7 carries Aero to its final form, and its default wallpaper combines light, bubbles, grass, and a butterfly with the brand mark.

context: Windows Aero was the design language of Windows Vista (2006) and Windows 7 (2009). Windows 7 refined it with larger window buttons and revised taskbar thumbnails; Windows 8 replaced it with the flat Metro language. [Wikipedia: Windows Aero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windows_Aero).

Avcı writes that “with Windows 7, the final form of the Aero interface was established,” and uses the Windows 7 default wallpaper as the emblem of the “Aero” half of the style’s name. [Avcı 2024, “Physical reflections of digital aesthetics”](https://doi.org/10.17932/IAU.EJNM.25480200.2024/ejnm_v8i3003), pp. 461 and 464.

Wikipedia says Windows 7 “expanded on” the characteristics that Vista introduced, and that the style waned in the early 2010s and was replaced by flat design. [Wikipedia: Frutiger Aero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frutiger_Aero).
observed: The wallpaper is a saturated blue field. The four-pane Windows flag glows in orange, green, blue, and yellow at its center.
The flag panes hold small nature motifs: grass blades, a butterfly, translucent bubbles, and a lens-flare highlight.
The Start menu and taskbar are translucent blue glass; the Start button is a round glossy orb.
In the window crop, the title bars are pale translucent glass; the close button is a glossy red rounded rectangle with a lighter top half.
interpretation: Where Vista is darker and more atmospheric, Windows 7 is brighter and more saturated. Its wallpaper is a compact list of the style’s motifs in one image.
borrow: Make one glossy accent control (for example a close or primary button) with a lighter upper half and a darker lower half.
Combine a brand mark with small nature details (bubbles, grass, a light flare) instead of abstract decoration.

references.title: Windows Vista Aero interface
references.lede: The desktop that gave the style half its name: tinted glass window frames over a green and blue aurora wallpaper.
references.summary: Glass window frames, a round Start orb, and an aurora wallpaper. Windows Vista, 2006–2007.
references.made: 2006 (released to manufacturing November 8, 2006; general release January 30, 2007)

evidence.note: Inspected the non-free 640 × 480 screenshot [File:Windows Vista.png](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Windows_Vista.png) (Windows Vista Ultimate with the Aero theme) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored. The operating system was not run.

styles.note: Windows Aero is the “Aero” in the style’s name, and scholars call Vista one of the first mature examples of the style.

context: Windows Aero is the design language introduced in Windows Vista in 2006 and continued in Windows 7. Its visual style emphasized “animation, glass, and translucency”; the name is a backronym for Authentic, Energetic, Reflective, and Open. [Wikipedia: Windows Aero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windows_Aero).
Windows Vista was released to manufacturing on November 8, 2006, and internationally on January 30, 2007. [Wikipedia: Windows Vista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windows_Vista).

Emirhan Avcı calls Vista’s Aero interface “one of the first mature examples of Frutiger Aero” and notes that Microsoft published an “Aero Aesthetics” guide for designers with Vista. [Avcı 2024, “Physical reflections of digital aesthetics”](https://doi.org/10.17932/IAU.EJNM.25480200.2024/ejnm_v8i3003), pp. 461–462.

The name Frutiger Aero joins the Frutiger typeface with Windows Aero. It was coined by Sofi Xian (then Sofi Lee) of the Consumer Aesthetics Research Institute in 2018. [Wikipedia: Frutiger Aero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frutiger_Aero); [CARI: Frutiger Aero](https://cari.institute/aesthetics/frutiger-aero).
observed: Window frames are translucent, blue-green tinted glass; the wallpaper shows through the title bar and borders.
The wallpaper is a dark green-to-teal field with luminous, curved light streaks, like an aurora.
The Start button is a round glossy orb at the bottom left; the taskbar is dark and glassy.
Sidebar gadgets on the right have rounded corners and soft shadows: an analog clock, a photo of a toucan, and a feed viewer.
Icons are detailed, shaded, and glossy (a globe, a padlock, a blue monitor).
interpretation: Vista is the reference point for the style’s surface grammar: glass instead of opaque chrome, light instead of line, and nature (aurora, toucan photo) placed inside a technical frame.
borrow: Use a thin, tinted translucent frame around content, with a lighter highlight along its top edge, rather than a solid title bar.
Place content on a dark-to-light luminous gradient with soft curved streaks instead of a flat background.

references.title: Zurich University of the Arts website
references.lede: The ZHdK home page hangs a bold Helvetica title and a list of large gray links from one strong left axis.
references.summary: Bold black Helvetica on white, hung from one left axis, with small right-aligned labels in the margin column.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 25 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. The English home page redirected to https://www.zhdk.ch/en/zurich-university-of-the-arts-1.

styles.note: A clear example from a Zurich design school: Helvetica only, a strong left axis, asymmetric margins, and black, white, and gray. It fails the `type.sizeRange` metric because most of the text on the page is large (see the style page).

observed: A small Z logo and the letters hdk sit at the top left, with the school’s German and English names in very small type between short horizontal dashes.
The title “Zurich University of the Arts” is set in two lines of large, bold black sans-serif, flush left.
A round pale-yellow badge at the top right reads “Subscribe to ZHdK’s event newsletter” in tilted text.
A thin gray rule separates the title from a section headed ZHdK.
Six links (Studying at ZHdK, Research, Continuing Education, Preparatory training, International, About us) are set large, bold, and gray, flush left on the same axis as the title.
In the left margin, the small labels ZHdK, News, and Events are aligned right, against the main axis.
interpretation: The measurement finds only Helvetica, square corners, no shadows, and one accent hue (the yellow badge). The base size is 45 px because the large links hold most of the characters, so the size range is only 1.89 even though the page has 10 px labels and an 85 px title.
The margin labels aligned right against the main text column are a direct Swiss-grid device: two columns meet at one shared axis.
borrow: Set section labels in a narrow margin column, aligned right, so that they meet the main column at one vertical line.
